title: Conducting Reliable Keyword Estimation with Unreliable ASR in Police Audio Data
summary: Extracting insights from large audio data sets using human transcription is expensive and time-consuming. Off-the-shelf Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems offer an easy-to-use scalable alternative, but systematic transcription errors, especially in domain-specific settings, can bias downstream analyses and lead to unreliable conclusions. We investigate whether imperfect ASR transcripts can still be used to obtain statistically valid keyword frequency estimates by combining model outputs with a small set of human-labeled examples, following Prediction Powered Inference and Design-based Supervised Learning frameworks. We evaluate this approach on police radio communications from Baltimore and Chicago, a domain in which keyword distributions could provide valuable insights into police activity, but off-the-shelf ASR systems exhibit systematic errors on operationally important terminology. Using bootstrap-based confidence interval coverage as our evaluation metric, we find that our approach substantially increases the number of domain-specific keywords that can be analyzed with statistically valid confidence intervals, from 43.0% using ASR alone and 27.2% using only a small set of human-labeled transcriptions to 56.2% in the Baltimore dataset, with similar improvements observed in Chicago data. Our results demonstrate that post-hoc error correction can improve statistical validity of downstream analyses even for poor-quality transcriptions, offering an avenue for better leveraging off-the-shelf ASR models for large-scale speech analysis.

title: Concerns in Benchmarking Jailbreaks: An Empirical Study of Attack Success Rates
summary: Jailbreak methods are commonly compared using Attack Success Rate (ASR), but these comparisons depend on how responses are generated and judged. In this paper, we examine eight attacks against three open-weight language models using three evaluation procedures. Low-resource language attacks achieve a mean ASR of 96.0% under keyword matching but 2.7% under a Qwen3 evaluator following StrongREJECT scoring instructions. Changing the number and arrangement of attempts reverses the ranking of DeepInception and rewriting. In a separate experiment, sampling 100 responses for each unchanged request at Ollama's default temperature of 0.8 yields 100% ASR under keyword matching but 50% under the Qwen3 evaluator. Beyond evaluator sensitivity, these findings raise a safety concern: repeated sampling can expose residual unsafe behavior despite an initial refusal, suggesting probabilistic suppression rather than robust exclusion. We recommend explicit success definitions, matched response budgets, validated evaluators, and reporting cumulative failure under repeated interaction rather than relying on single-generation tests.

title: WhatIf-Bench: Benchmarking Intervention-Aware Time Series Forecasting
summary: Recent time series foundation models (TSFMs) can consume covariates in-context, extending zero-shot forecasting to problems driven by external factors. This enables scenario analysis: forecasting how a target responds to events that set covariates to chosen future values. Whether they can do this reliably is an open question. We introduce WhatIf-Bench, a benchmark measuring how well forecasters use covariates to forecast a target's response to future events. WhatIf-Bench is semi-synthetic: time series come from mechanistic simulators of data centers, power grids, road traffic, and water networks, with controlled covariate-target relationships grounded in each system. Each task presents a history of events intervening on covariates, then asks to forecast a future event that either replays seen values (Replay) or sets them to unseen ones (Novel). Varying the number of covariates, historical events, and event length yields 37,665 tasks. Evaluating TSFMs, frontier LLMs, and simple regression baselines, we find the LLMs reach the highest skill (improvement over a naive baseline), ahead of the best TSFMs. Every model forecasts well on Replay futures (48 to 85% skill) but drops to -7 to 50% on Novel futures, with the regression baselines falling the most. Skill on Novel futures also falls as events set more covariates jointly. More historical events raise skill on Novel futures across the board, but large differences remain. WhatIf-Bench reveals generalization to Novel futures as the core challenge, and offers a testbed toward arbitrary scenario analysis.

title: Reward Objectives for Robust (PO)MDPs: A Law-Preserving Equivalence with (Partially Observable) Games
summary: Robust partially observable Markov decision processes model agents that act under partial observability while adversarial environment resolves uncertainty in the transition probabilities. Reward objectives such as discounted-sum, long-run average and cumulative reward under finite and infinite horizons allow quantifying the utility of an agent. We consider the problem of solving RPOMDPs under all four reward objectives, where the goal is to decide whether the value of a risk measure with respect to a reward objective exceeds a given threshold. We consider different risk measures, such as (1)~expected value, (2)~mean-variance (MV), (3)~conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and (4)~entropic risk (ERisk). Our results can be summarized as follows. First, we formalize the class of law-invariant risk measures, that subsume all four risk measures above. Second, we propose a unified framework for solving RPOMDPs with discounted-sum, long-run average and cumulative reward objectives under any law-invariant risk measure, by reducing the problem to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs). Our unified framework applies to (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, which we show to be {\em equivalent} to POSGs, for each of the four reward objectives and any law-invariant risk measure. We prove equivalence by designing logspace reductions between the RPOMDP and POSG models, that map strategies to strategies and preserve the distribution of the reward objective, up to a constant rescaling factor. Third, as a corollary, we derive new computational complexity results for R(PO)MDPs and POSGs. In particular, we show that solving (s,a)-rectangular RMDPs is as hard as solving simple stochastic games.

title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents
summary: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.

title: Agentic Orchestration of EDC Data Space Retrieval and Natural Language Driven Data Processing
summary: Participating in a data space still requires the Dataspace Protocol (DSP) negotiation flow to be hand-coded against each provider's access policy. We present a multi-agent architecture that automates this process using natural language requests. Built on LangGraph over an Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC), the design separates concerns into cooperating agents. The orchestrator's role is to route and plan. The data extraction agent's role is to expose the DSP protocol's three composable tools (catalog discovery, contract negotiation and download). The agent also gates negotiations on the consumers' verifiable credentials, refusing assets rather than fabricating them. Furthermore, there are downstream Machine Learning (ML) and Visualization agents, as well as a final Verification agent, which confirms that the request was actually fulfilled and rechecks the intended operation against the contract's usage policy. In a primary benchmark involving 600 runs, the system achieved 89% task success with zero policy violations when evaluating multi-dimensional policy reasoning with a locally hosted open-weight model. It failed safely through refusal rather than misrouting. The reliability of the system is largely dependent on the phrasing of requests: technical and expert requests succeed up to 98% of the time, whereas casual and under-specified requests succeed 72% of the time. Furthermore, in a secondary evaluation of 600 runs isolating hierarchical geographic access control, the framework successfully blocks 100% of unauthorized regional requests. While the verification agent hallucinates that 1% of these requests, the system logs confirm that no data is ever extracted and the framework simultaneously achieves an end-to-end verified delivery rate of 86% for eligible consumers.

title: Autonomous intelligence for mining productivity: a multi-agent AI approach to operational value creation
summary: Integrated Remote Operation Centres (IROCs) are emerging as the architectural frontier of Industry 4.0 for capital-intensive sectors such as mining, oil and gas, and energy. Yet two intertwined gaps constrain their evolution towards full autonomy. First, no integrated agentic architecture has been proposed for mining IROCs that orchestrates Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems, digital twins, predictive analytics and human-machine interfaces under safety-critical constraints. Second, no evaluation framework jointly addresses the real-time, Health-Safety-Environment, regulatory-auditability and cost-per-decision requirements that govern industrial agentic deployments. This paper makes four contributions. It synthesises industry needs and quantified gains documented in analogous industries that motivate an agentic approach to mining IROCs. It introduces EI2ROC, a three-tier multi-agent architecture combining a Large Language Model orchestrator with specialised monitoring and production-capacityprediction agents communicating through a Model Context Protocol-style tool interface. It provides a critical review of agentic evaluation along six orthogonal dimensions and identifies the industrial blind spot of current benchmarks. Finally, it proposes a multi-dimensional benchmarking framework for industrial agentic AI comprising scenario library, harness, metrics and humancalibration protocol. The paper states explicitly which components are implemented in the current prototype, which belong to the proposed reference design and which remain future work, and reports preliminary cost and latency observations from an operating site. Together, EI2ROC and the benchmarking framework constitute a methodological blueprint transferable across CAPEX intensive industries.

title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent system's performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the human-developed instruct model's 55.4%. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTrainingBench.

title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
summary: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.

title: Heartbeat Thinking: Speculative Reasoning and Tool Execution While Listening in Realtime Voice Agents
summary: Tool-using voice agents often leave users waiting after speech ends, even when actionable information arrives earlier in the request. Speculative approaches begin work during speech, but chunk-bounded or interrupt-on-update generation can truncate a tool call before its arguments are complete. This couples computation time to speech updates, limiting useful work completed in advance. We introduce Heartbeat Thinking, which handles updated input through new Thinker invocations while allowing ongoing invocations and dispatched tools to finish. Periodic invocations read the latest partial transcript and a shared record of completed reasoning and tool results. These results help resolve missing arguments and initiate dependent calls, allowing preparation to progress across speech updates. Across SpeechFCEval, FDBench v3, and AudioCRAG, Heartbeat improves aggregate speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse over a SHANKS-style windowed baseline, with benchmark-dependent effects on final task quality. On FDBench v3, it increases tool coverage by 16 percentage points and reduces mean final-response latency by 36.4\%. The results show that heartbeat thinking paradigm preserving ongoing computation during speech can turn listening time into reusable preparation for faster and more capable voice-agent responses.

title: VISAGENT: An Agent-Based End-to-End Voice Interaction System
summary: Voice-based public services have evolved from manual switchboards to intelligent platforms to meet modern user needs. However, current systems remain constrained by rigid menu-driven interaction, fragmented vertical services, and limited extensibility. To address these issues, we present VISAGENT, an agent-based end-to-end voice interaction system for large-scale public services that integrates end-to-end speech interaction, hierarchical agent routing, a scalable voice-agent marketplace, and user memory support. The system replaces menu-driven workflows with natural speech and dynamically dispatches user requests to either a general conversational model or specialized domain agents via a two-level routing paradigm that achieves sub-second intent-to-agent selection over hundreds of agents. User memory informs preference-aware agent selection and supplies relevant preferences and context to selected agents, supporting personalized task execution and reducing the need for users to repeat previously provided information. A voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational entities, enabling dynamic onboarding and ecosystem-level extensibility. We validate VISAGENT through a real-world deployment in China's 114 hotline across multiple service domains. Experimental results demonstrate low-latency full-duplex interaction, robust routing scalability, and competitive speech naturalness. More broadly, this work advocates a shift from isolated voice assistants toward agent-centric conversational infrastructures, providing a general blueprint for building extensible voice-agent systems in public services and beyond.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Expands beyond Text to Support Code, Images, Video, and Audio
summary:
Based on Gemma 4 and released under the Apache 2.0 license, Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-weight, multimodal embedding model designed to make semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) more efficient while optimizing performance for on-device deployment.

By Sergio De Simone

title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents
summary: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.

title: Not All Similarity Is Leakage: Distribution-Aware Identity Leakage Assessment in Synthetic Face Datasets
summary: Synthetic data provides the means for more ethical and less biased facial recognition. Nonetheless, the limitations of generative models and the conditioning process they rely on pose a risk of identity leakage, resulting in synthetic samples that are overly similar to those seen in a generator's training set, mitigating privacy benefits. In this work, we show that previously proposed approaches are affected by two key limitations: high classifier dependence and a tendency to identify leakage with respect to real datasets that were not used in training. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel metric called Scaled Overlap (SO), which adapts a non-parametric data-copying test for facial recognition and extends it to the identity level. By leveraging a multi-model setup that compensates for errors in individual classifiers, it provides insights into the true strength of identity leakage. Our analysis identifies leaking datasets (CemiFace, SFace2, IDNet) with the most acute leakage introduced by generative model conditioning in CemiFace, demonstrates that real datasets do not contribute equally to generator training, and shows that the majority of synthetic images are drawn from multiple identities rather than relying on a single identity. Ultimately, our study provides new insights into the quality of synthetic datasets and gives more reliable techniques to help the community ensure the trustworthiness of synthetic data.

title: FinHopper: A Progressive Multi-Hop Benchmark for Complex Financial Agents with Step-wise Evaluation
summary: Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. This strict answer-conditioned dependency makes small intermediate errors cascade into plausible but wrong search trajectories. We introduce FinHopper, a benchmark for complex financial agents with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops, covering stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, with gold intermediate answers for process-level evaluation. To construct FinHopper at scale, we design a state-transition-based synthesis framework that composes verified atomic financial QA patterns into dependency-preserving chains, followed by targeted in-synthesis verification, model-ensemble checking, and public-search validation by financial experts. Experiments with 20 LLM-agent configurations show that public search tools are necessary but insufficient: performance drops sharply as hop depth increases, the best model remains far below human experts, and process-aware scoring reveals partial reasoning progress hidden by final-answer-only evaluation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/justajustin/FinHopper/.

title: SPLASH: Contrastive Audit Pressure for Detecting and Localizing Security Hallucinations in Generated Code
summary: Code generated by large language models often passes every functional test while remaining insecure. These security hallucinations are common, written with high confidence, and repeated across samples, so neither the generator's own uncertainty nor static analyzers reliably catch them. We introduce SPLASH, which is guided by a new measure called audit pressure. It contrasts teacher-forced log-probabilities for the generated program under a security review and a style review. Aggregated to statements and programs, and grounded in a probabilistic model of competing edits, audit pressure allows SPLASH to choose the secure program among a model's candidate programs and locate the vulnerable statement, with no model training, CWE-specific rules, or internal access to the generating model. On 63,684 programs generated by 12 models for 899 tasks, SPLASH picks secure code in 74% of cases, places the vulnerable statement first in 58% of insecure programs, and chooses better than a frontier LLM judge.

title: NIOCIS: Typed-Decision Next-Hop Routing with Node-Conditioned Option Spaces for Tool-Use Agents
summary: Tool-use agents pay per decision: at each hop a language model re-reads the state and thinks for seconds, though its actions are finite and decisions recur. We present NIOCIS, a routing layer that folds execution logs into a loop-collapsed action graph (forward transitions plus recovery back-edges) answering one typed question: which declared option at a state, plus stop, does the fleet take next? A small model reads a calibrated distribution over them in one pass, emitting no text. On 1,615 production security-operations episodes we measure what the layer replaces, returns and is bounded by. Replaces: the typed encoder matches the logged next hop on 32.2% of the 3,875 held-out decisions (34.9% within the declared options) in 10 ms of encoder time (19.5 ms for the typed-choice form), against 2.2 s per LLM hop; two feature readouts reach 32.8% and 32.3%, an ordering the paired test does not resolve, so the typed layer is chosen for cost, not a separated lead. Tuning: jpt-4b reaches 9.9% zero-shot and 31.9% fine-tuned, a gap an exact paired test does not resolve (p=0.68), at 244 ms. Returns little: the realised hop falls outside the declared options for 7.9% of decisions and outside the model's top twenty for 9.3%; the most confident 15% holds 91.9% accuracy. Bounded: a cross-trace leave-one-out test puts the released state's ceiling at 25.6--44.9% as the state key grows more specific, i.e. repeated states disagree more often than they agree; the option-space ablation attributes the gain to per-node candidate restriction (+3.5 points over a flat catalog) rather than graph traversal (zero within its interval); a gated self-evolution loop lifts every arm above its anchor yet ends below full supervision; a confidence-gated cascade loses agreement when the escalation arm is the zero-shot stand-in; and agreement past a third of the fleet needs a state carrying the plan and the observation.

title: Behavioral Probes for Information Flow in LLM Swarms
summary: Most existing approaches to LLM swarm optimization are utility-driven, focusing on final task utility while leaving the processing, integration, and reliance of information within individual interactions largely implicit. To address this, we study LLM swarm interactions from an information-flow-based view and introduce behavioral probes to quantify information flow patterns. Specifically, we repurpose External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS)---originally designed for hallucination analysis---to measure a node's external-context dependence and parametric-knowledge dependence, respectively. Across controlled and realistic swarm settings, we observe consistent patterns: ECS increases with input relevance and distinguishes useful multi-source contributions, while PKS decreases as informative context accumulates. Building on this heuristic interpretation, we demonstrate how these probes can complement utility-driven structure optimization in two controlled applications. Probe-guided node pruning reduces redundant communication and token consumption, and probe-guided reasoning-path search accelerates convergence compared to utility-only baselines. Our empirical results suggest that behavioral probes can make the internal information flow of LLM swarms observable and serve as effective auxiliary signals for structure optimization.

title: Token-Set Choice Confounds POPE: A Systematic Audit of Yes/No Extraction in VLM Hallucination Evaluation
summary: We set out to reproduce a recent hallucination-mitigation result on the POPE benchmark. The LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline we measured, 82.21 F1 on the adversarial split, sat 1.21 to 8.67 points above the adversarial baselines we planned to compare against (81.00, 79.30, and 73.54). We looked at the evaluation code and found a readout choice that moves F1 on its own. A two-token logit readout decides yes versus no by comparing two vocabulary IDs, 3582 ("yes") and 1217 ("no"). Across 9,000 greedy-decode questions spanning all three splits, neither ID is generated even once. The model emits " Yes" (token 3869) and " No" (token 1939), because SentencePiece prepends a space byte after the prompt suffix "ASSISTANT:". Read with an eight-token lookup that covers the space-prefixed surface forms, LLaVA-1.5-7B scores F1 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on the adversarial, popular, and random splits. That 6.13-point adversarial shift exceeds the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed. None of them states its readout, and our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, so we cannot say how much of any reported gain a matched evaluation would keep. That comparison stays unresolved until readout and precision are matched. On the fixed baseline we run nine inference-time corrections of our own (none beat it) and dissect why the adversarial split resists logit-level intervention. In a 3,000-question probe, wrong predictions draw more image attention than correct ones (Cohen's $d=-0.46$, $p=1.4\times10^{-24}$), the opposite of what grounding-based corrections assume. A four-readout audit across four further VLMs from three tokenizer families confirms the confound is protocol-level, not model-specific: porting the LLaVA-1.5 IDs verbatim drops F1 to 0.00 on the two disjoint-vocabulary models, whereas a tokenizer-derived readout holds between 0.80 and 0.92.

title: CXBench: A Benchmark for Process-Compliant LLM Agents in Regulated Customer-Experience Workflows
summary:
Tool-using language agents increasingly perform regulated customer-service workflows, where a correct final state is insufficient: agents must also provide disclosures, obtain consent, and follow required procedures. Existing tool-agent benchmarks largely score final business states, accepting trajectories that reach correct outcomes through non-compliant processes.
  We introduce cxbench, a benchmark that evaluates outcome and process compliance separately across six regulated domains. Each task combines a customer request, a tool-based environment, and explicit process requirements. Rule cards link cited regulatory obligations to observable trace evidence. A hybrid grader combines deterministic checks for ordering and authority with an LLM judge for semantic requirements. We define a false-pass as an outcome-pass run that fails process checks.
  Across seven models and 120 tasks, 55.5% of the 840 retained executions are false-passes, representing 80.1% of outcome-passing runs; only 13.8% pass both checks. Process-inclusive evaluation changes the observed model ordering and exposes differences hidden by outcome-only scoring. cxbench makes these failures inspectable through trace-linked criteria.

title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
summary: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.

title: EvoSkill v2: Fully Agentic Skill Evolution from Benchmark Adaptation to a Stateful Evolver
summary: EvoSkill v2 is a three-agent system that edits the instructions (skills) an agent is given, leaving its model and harness intact. The user starts a run by describing a benchmark and supplying a grader, which a benchmark adaptor turns into a benchmark-specific plugin. A solver attempts the tasks, and an evolver reads the solver's training rollouts and rewrites the skills at each epoch. We implement the evolver as one stateful coding agent with a bash tool for the whole run, unlike the two most common designs among the skill optimizers we surveyed: a sequence of single model calls, as in SkillOpt, and an agent that starts afresh each round, as in SkillBoost. We also measure how much the solver's rollouts vary from one attempt to the next, give the evolver several attempts per training task, and accept every epoch's skills instead of selecting among them on noisy scores. With fine-grained ground truth, EvoSkill v2's skills raised the held-out pass rate above the stronger of SkillOpt and SkillBoost by 7.7 percentage points on SpreadsheetBench v2 and by 5.4 on $τ^3$-bench banking. In both benchmarks and both feedback settings, EvoSkill v2's evolver cost less per percentage point of held-out pass rate gained than either baseline's optimizer. EvoSkill v2 also enables a less capable model to improve its own skills, demonstrated by a gain of up to 21.5 percentage points in the $τ^3$-bench banking experiment where Claude Haiku 5.5 powers both solver and evolver.

title: Google named a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Agentic AI Platforms
summary:
As organizations work to leverage AI to transform their businesses, it is clear that the raw model intelligence is not the key challenge.

Consistently, we hear that the challenges lie in how the agents can be deployed across the company while meeting key requirements for quality, integration, security, and governance.

Gemini provides that connected foundation across the enterprise, and it’s why we believe Google was named a Leader in the inaugural IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Agentic AI Platforms 2026 Vendor Assessment1.

Gemini meets work where it already happens

A viable agentic platform has to meet work where it already happens – and run under production-grade controls. Gemini is engineered to deliver developer velocity without compromising governance, built around four core differentiators:

1. Surfaces that connect builders and business teams

Gemini makes it so that every surface connects back to one universal foundation.

  • Where teams already work: Employees collaborate with Gemini directly inside Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or team chats – the agent carries the same persistent memory, skills, and enterprise permissions across desktop and mobile without needing to switch tools.
  • Builder tools centered on choice: Gemini platform supports how developers want to work, spanning no-code and low-code builders in the studio to code-first workflows with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) and Antigravity.
  • Workflows that compound across the organization: When a team solves a complex workflow, they can package it into a shared skill published to a central Agent Registry. Gemini calls on these skills directly to execute tasks, turning proven procedures into reusable assets across the entire company.

2. Radical openness across models, enterprise data, and tools

Gemini adapts to the software you already run, not the other way around.

  • Model choice: Through Model Garden in Gemini platform, teams have direct access to over 200 models – including all of the breakthroughs from Google DeepMind like Gemini 4 Argon, day one access to the latest Anthropic models, and third-party and open models.
  • Grounding on your enterprise data: Gemini connects directly to live enterprise data across Google Cloud in BigQuery and Cloud Storage, as well as Salesforce, SAP, and others. Because Gemini inherits each employee's existing credentials, sensitive information stays governed at the source.
  • Open standards: Built on open protocols like MCP and A2A, Gemini can easily plug into your existing toolchains and communicate across multi-vendor environments.

3. Smarter token economics

Gemini optimizes cost, latency, and performance directly at the execution layer.

  • Matching tasks to the right model: By default, Gemini uses Auto mode for users, letting the platform match each step of a task to the right model dynamically. It defaults to a fast workhorse model like Gemini Flash, and escalates to a high-capacity frontier reasoning model only when task complexity requires it.
  • Reusable skills: Teams can package proven processes into shared skills. Your agents can execute against these established procedures, improving consistency and reducing repetitive token consumption across the company.
  • Budget guardrails: Administrators can set spending limits by project, department, or individual agent in the billing console. When a budget threshold is reached, new requests pause while active tasks are allowed to complete, giving finance and engineering predictable cost controls without abruptly interrupting in-progress work.

4. Built-in governance and security

Gemini incorporates enterprise governance natively, and at no additional cost.

  • Dedicated agent identity: Every agent receives its own distinct, authenticated identity governed by least-privilege permissions. When an agent takes action, every event is recorded in an audit trail tied directly to that identity and the identity of which user was using the agent for the task.
  • Isolated sandboxes: A sandboxed boundary keeps dynamic tasks strictly contained, protecting your underlying infrastructure, core network, and sensitive corporate data from being exposed or compromised.
  • Policy enforcement: Rather than relying on a model to self-police, Agent Gateway automatically applies corporate security policies, blocks data leakage, and ensures agents only access what they are explicitly authorized to touch.

Looking forward

At its core, Gemini is all about giving your organization an open, reliable platform where builders have choice and teams work with complete confidence.

We are honored by IDC MarketScape’s recognition of Google as a Leader, and we look forward to continuing this work alongside our customers.

Download the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Agentic AI Platforms 2026 Vendor Assessment excerpt to learn why Google is named a Leader.

title: MASIF: Implicit Failures for Process Observability in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can complete a task despite local execution errors that are corrected, bypassed, or carried forward without individually determining its outcome. We call these implicit failures (IFs) and study them as signals for process observability beyond final task outcome. Across 1,828 traces from nine MAS-benchmark configurations, IFs occur in 54.3% of successful and 75.2% of failed traces. We develop taxonomies of error types and subsequent absorption mechanisms, supported by human and cross-model annotation audits. Counterfactual replay further probes how repairing an IF changes the final outcome. To examine the practical value of IFs, we evaluate IF-based best-of-N trace selection against existing process reward models, and introduce a novel RL algorithm, IF-GRPO, that uses IF costs to refine preferences among successful trajectories in GRPO. Experiments show that IF-GRPO exhibits some gains in accuracy and process metrics. Importantly, it exposes trade-offs between task performance, IF count and cost, and token-normalized IF density. Overall, our results show that IFs provide complementary process observability into how MAS reach their outcomes, including error recovery, propagation, and IF-based process differences that final task success alone does not expose.

title: Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in Large Language Models
summary: Whether a language model "knows what it knows" matters for trustworthy deployment and for deciding when it should abstain. Prior work usually measures this through one channel: verbalized confidence, a linear probe on hidden states, or agreement among sampled answers (semantic entropy), and often treats these as interchangeable. We compare all three in a pre-registered audit of five Qwen2.5 models (0.5B-7B, including a base/instruct pair at 7B) on factual retrieval (PopQA, SimpleQA) and multi-step reasoning (GSM8K, MATH). First, probes trained on prefill states to predict whether sampled answers will disagree become informative earlier for retrieval (about 7% of layer depth on average) than for reasoning (about 28%). The pre-registered five-layer test supported this only marginally; a finer 21-layer follow-up, designed after those results, supports it more clearly. In most retrieval cells, however, a prompt-only TF-IDF classifier matches the probe, so the early signal may reflect surface features of the question. Second, verbalized confidence is unstable: slightly different prompt templates yield scores that barely correlate. Third, Expected Calibration Error is misleading: verbal confidence looks well calibrated because it clusters near the base rate while discriminating poorly, whereas sampling agreement has worse ECE but about twice the resolution. Of five pre-registered hypotheses, two were falsified, one was partly supported, one was not supported, and one could not be tested because the base model's verbal confidence was degenerate.

title: OV-PEAR: Observation-Verified Pose-Scale Estimation and Reconstruction for Unknown Industrial Manipulation Objects
summary: Fine industrial robotic manipulation requires 6D pose, scale, and an operation-ready 3D model. Existing industrial pose estimation relies on CAD models, object-specific training data, or stable workcells, limiting use with unseen objects; zero-shot methods suffer from single-view occlusion, generative bias, and scale uncertainty. We present OV-PEAR, an observation-verified framework for 3D reconstruction and pose-scale estimation of unknown industrial objects. Its three-stage object-centric pipeline: (1) segments RGB-D instances and generates object-level 3D hypotheses; (2) anchors them to the robot frame via appearance-aware view retrieval, explicit scale search, and visibility-sensitive registration; (3) back-projects multi-view RGB-D evidence into the object-canonical frame to verify voxel occupancy, suppress hallucinations, and produce reusable trusted object models. On BOP-Industrial, OV-PEAR achieves 0.657 average AR and improves pose and voxel-level geometric consistency in real scenes; real-robot connector assembly reaches 99.67% grasp and 84.00% assembly success. The model library and pose-scale log enable short-term object-level state maintenance at 0.02 ms/frame.

title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models
summary: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.

title: When to Stop Asking: Factor Coverage Bias and LLM Determinability Judgments with Underspecified Information in Medicine
summary: Clinical decision-making often begins with underspecified information and requires not only gathering missing information but also knowing when to stop. This calls for judging determinability (whether the available information is sufficient for a decision) by considering whether missing information could change the conclusion, not simply the amount of available decision-relevant information. Reliance on this amount as a cue for determinability, which we term \textit{factor coverage bias}, could undermine the trustworthiness of large language models (LLMs) through premature conclusions or excessive information gathering, such as unnecessary invasive tests. Yet whether LLMs exhibit this bias remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we construct a controlled pairwise benchmark in which LLMs identify the determinable case within each determinable--undeterminable pair. We add a decision-relevant factor to either side while keeping each case's determinability unchanged, and similarly add irrelevant text to distinguish this bias from context-length effects. Adding a relevant factor made LLMs more likely to select the augmented case as determinable even when it remained undeterminable, an effect that persisted with increased reasoning effort, while adding irrelevant text made them less likely to select the augmented case, an effect that reasoning substantially reduced. These findings identify factor coverage bias as a failure mode distinct from context-length effects and a potential risk to LLM trustworthiness. Our work provides an evaluation framework for LLM trustworthiness under underspecification.

title: ActTime: Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series
summary: Time-series models increasingly condition on known future inputs. In controlled systems, some of these inputs are actions that can be changed, compared, and optimized before execution. A model must therefore do more than predict the realized future: it must predict how outcomes change under different actions from the same observed history and support reliable comparison of candidate plans. We introduce ActTime, an action-conditioned world model for time series. Over the observed history, ActTime updates variable-specific latent states through an action-conditioned transition and corrects them using observations. It then rolls the same transition forward under candidate actions to generate future trajectories. Training uses only factual trajectories, without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision. We construct a simulator-grounded evaluation suite across building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory management, covering factual prediction, intervention-effect prediction, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. ActTime ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings. Across eight methods, the mean pairwise model-ranking reversal rate is 17.8% between factual prediction and intervention fidelity, and rises to 28.4% between intervention fidelity and decision ranking. These results show that factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality are related but not interchangeable.

title: Does Unlearning Survive Collaboration? Robust Unlearning for Shared-Model LLM Teams
summary: LLM unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities. As LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems, forgetting must remain effective during collaboration. Despite advances in forgetting effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness to relearning, team deployment remains underexplored. We find that collaboration weakens forgetting: final-answer evaluations miss recoverable evidence in team messages, including complementary clues supporting joint recovery. We establish theoretically and confirm empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. To address this challenge, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning (ACU). ACU trains a shared model using reconstruction feedback from individual and pooled messages, prioritizes views with higher recovery risk, and uses replacement-based credit assignment while protecting direct and collaborative utility. TOFU evaluates trajectory-level recovery, while WMDP-bio tests native forgetting and retained utility. On TOFU, ACU lowers full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. These results demonstrate that ACU curbs information leakage in LLM teams and generalizes across team sizes and readers.

title: ToolOPD: Credit-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Tool-Use Agents
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) enhances the capabilities of small language agents by providing dense, token-level supervision from a teacher model on student-generated trajectories. However, standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, assigning the same strength of teacher supervision to different actions. Through credit-distribution analysis and outcome-reversal counterfactual experiments, we find that trajectory credit is concentrated on a small number of critical actions. Moreover, even when the trajectory is held fixed, reversing only the final outcome substantially changes the credit assigned to multiple interaction turns. These findings show that the uniform-credit assumption fails to identify critical decisions and ultimately degrades the model's reasoning accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose ToolOPD, an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework designed for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD first summarizes each completed trajectory and its outcome into a reusable hindsight skill. It then measures how this skill changes the teacher's probability of each student action token and converts the change into outcome-aware credit. The resulting credit preserves supervision that supports successful decisions or discourages failed ones, while suppressing irrelevant and conflicting signals. ToolOPD uses these credits to reweight the action-level distillation loss and jointly optimizes it with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across multiple long-horizon tool interaction benchmarks demonstrate that ToolOPD significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines.

title: MT-CC: Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Asymmetric Calibration Behavior in Class-Incremental Learning
summary: As deep neural networks are required to continuously adapt to evolving data, class-incremental learning (CIL) has become an active research area. However, most existing works primarily focus on improving accuracy while overlooking confidence calibration, which measures the trustworthiness of the model's predictions. Although temperature scaling (TS) is effective for static calibration, it has rarely been explored in continual settings where data distributions evolve over time. In this paper, we introduce Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Continual Calibration (MT-CC), a novel post-hoc calibration framework that addresses the asymmetric calibration behavior in CIL, where the rate of confidence changes does not align with the rate of accuracy degradation across tasks, leading to different levels of miscalibration. Our key contribution is to design multiple temperature parameters through a lightweight grouping network that separates samples by confidence statistics and task-aware signals in CIL. Furthermore, a Groupwise Difference-between-Confidence-and-Accuracy (GDCA) regularization is incorporated to promote intra-group consistency. Experiments demonstrate that MT-CC significantly improves calibration performance while maintaining accuracy, offering a principled framework for reliable continual learning.

title: Zephyrus-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Weather Reporting
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times before producing a report. We use annotations from three meteorologists to audit the claim labels produced by our LLM judges. Finally, a curriculum helps small models first develop tool use and scientific reasoning through RL on verifiable weather-analysis questions, then optimize the open-ended report reward. After training Qwen3.5-4B with Zephyrus-R1, we improve the mean across six judge-metric scores by 26% over the base model and achieve results competitive with frontier open-weight models. For Qwen3.8-27B, we improve the same mean by 13% over the base model, by 6.7% over Kimi-K3, and by 2.7% over GPT-5.6-Luna.

title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
summary: State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads.

title: Assertion and Belief: Moore's Paradox in Language Models
summary: Moore's paradox \citep{moore1942} concerns sentences such as ``It is raining, but I don't believe that it is,'' which may well be true yet cannot be sensibly asserted. The absurdity lies not in the content but in the act, since to assert is to vouch for one's own belief. This makes the paradox a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning. We present the first test of Moore's paradox in LLMs, evaluating 12 models on a curated set of Moorean sentences in varied contexts. We find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, and that the judgement is not tied to a memorized form and tracks the speech act. Using the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; \citealt{goodmanfrank2016}), we then test whether these judgements arise from a listener reasoning about a speaker. We find the models' own listeners do not reason about their own speakers, and their reasoning traces suggest that they instead recall knowledge about the paradox and apply rules therein. The models thus appear to have learned the paradox as a fact about sentences, not as a requirement on speakers.

title: Representations in Motion: Layer-wise Rotation and Trajectory Divergence in LLMs
summary: Recent work suggests that activation dynamics--how representations change during inference--might be more revealing about language model behavior than static readouts from individual layers. In this work, we investigate the layer-wise evolution of representations of factuality, using true and false statements when the model is prompted to either lie or to be honest. We report a geometric phenomenon in which the factuality directions extracted from the lying and honest conditions appear to rotate away from each other across layers. We find that such layer-wise rotation also occurs in a task that requires the model to take different visual perspectives in the 3D world, suggesting that the rotation phenomenon might be indicative of manipulating conceptual spaces in general, rather than unique to factuality. We then investigate the "real time" transformation of conceptual representations on a trial-to-trial basis. We show that it is possible to make strong predictions about the model's target task and behavior from trajectories alone. In addition, diverging points in single-trial trajectories correspond to the onset of rotation in aggregated-trial analysis. Finally, we show that both rotation and divergent trajectories occur in more naturalistic settings in which models are not overtly prompted to "lie" but rather report false statements in the course of completing a different task.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
summary: A synopsis in novels folds a story into a few lines; a function in code gathers many steps with a single execution. Context editing is native to language itself. In this paper, we propose the Native Context Editing (NCE) framework, which gives language model agents a grammar for natively editing their own context. By encoding context-editing operations in a grammar of dedicated special tokens, we teach the agents to invoke edits through the language itself. We train agents on iteratively constructed trajectory segments, with each teacher edit conditioned on the evolving context. This establishes context editing as an atomic and inherent capability of LLM agents, enabling them to dynamically modify their context as they generate responses over long-horizon reasoning and interaction. Compared with context-editing methods that learn to generate tool-use code within specific external harness environments, our approach integrates context editing as an internal mechanism of the model's native generation process, enabling better generalization across diverse real-world workflows. On four long-horizon agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and SWE-bench Pro), NCE improves the average task success rate over the base model by 5.6 percentage points for LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse and by 4.5 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, while reducing average token usage by 36% and 15%, respectively.

title: DiaLong: Benchmarking Reminiscence in Long-Context Dialogues
summary: How well can transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) retain and recall memories in long contexts of dialogue? LLMs are known to forget long-range factual information in their context, yet the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to quantitatively assess these shortcomings. We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. It consists of 100 unique conversations created by humans and then augmented with LLMs, extending beyond lengths found in existing datasets. Our selected memory task is fact recall: classify 40 candidate facts about a dialogue as true or false. This task directly probes the model's ability to actively retain and retrieve information, serving as a critical measure of memory within extended conversational contexts. In testing both the latest LLMs and proposed memory enhancements on DiaLong, we demonstrate that more work needs to be done to enable LLMs with better memory performance. By enhancing memory capabilities, LLMs can improve in maintaining coherence, relevance, and human-like interaction over extended conversation. Improving these capabilities will help LLMs fulfill diverse user needs and expectations in various conversational scenarios.

title: Mixture-of-Memories: Low-Overhead Language Modeling with Modular Knowledge Injection
summary: Large language models store substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, yet this knowledge is difficult to control, update, and reliably elicit at inference time. Existing memory-augmented approaches typically rely on a single auxiliary mechanism, such as retrieval, parameter updates, or neural memory, and therefore apply the same form of correction to tokens with very different knowledge demands. We propose Mixture-of-Memories (MoM), a memory-augmented language modeling framework that separates routed neural memory from writable factual memory. MoM combines a frozen base LM with two neural memory experts: a latent memory that provides low-latency hidden-state corrections and a lexical memory that provides a token-space knowledge pathway. A lightweight Budget Router sets per-token mixture weights from uncertainty and disagreement features, replacing the fixed interpolation of prior memory modules. For post-hoc updates, an external explicit memory stays outside the router, because a router trained before facts are written learns to down-weight it; new facts are appended without retraining any component and used only when an answer-level gate accepts the retrieved fact. Experiments across language modeling, factual QA, update analysis, and efficiency show that MoM improves both predictive accuracy and updateability while retaining low inference overhead.

title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences
summary: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. We propose ArabPref, which to our knowledge is the first large-scale pan-Arab preference data set for the alignment of cultural behavior conditioned on the country. Our contribution includes two resources in English and Modern Standard Arabic: a culturally grounded preference dataset for training and evaluation, and a multiple-choice benchmark designed to assess culturally aligned behavior across nations. All test data are validated by native speakers to ensure authenticity. To optimize cultural alignment, we experiment with post-training methods across multilingual and Arabic-centric language models, evaluating performance on both generation tasks and our cultural multiple-choice benchmark. By releasing an evaluation benchmark, we provide a foundation for systematically studying and improving culturally aligned behavior in language models.

title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
summary: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. To address this gap, we introduce TREK, a suite of three components: TREKTRACE is a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific stages of retrieval and reasoning. We apply it to TREKBENCH-WILD, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions that require complex reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge. Surprisingly, the main bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving all the information needed to answer. To study this bottleneck, we build TREKBENCH-CTRL, a controlled benchmark with distractors spanning temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness, and show that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty. Together, TREK provides a testbed for diagnosing and improving reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge.

title: Assessing the Empirical Evidence for Loss of Control from Agentic General-Purpose AI
summary: Theoretical literature warns that advanced generalist agentic systems might pursue instrumental goals that are misaligned with human preferences, thus posing risks of irreversible loss of human control. The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI lists loss of control as a systemic risk that must be assessed, yet no structured assessment of the quality of the empirical evidence for this risk exists. This study fills that gap. We evaluate 19 recent empirical studies across eight properties identified from threat models (such as strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication), assessing the quality of evidence across three dimensions: construct validity, content validity, and external validity. Our central finding is that the current body of evidence supports a judgment of loss of control as "weakly plausible." In our framework, 'plausibility' denotes the strength and direction of available evidence, not a probability estimate. Emerging evidence exists across multiple properties. No study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment that a property is present; a single study clears them only for a negative-direction judgment (against situational awareness). Validity gaps, particularly in external validity, are widespread. Therefore, our findings highlight the need for more rigorous evaluations of agentic general-purpose AI systems. However, for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices, reflecting a ceiling on feasible evidence rather than absence of the capability. Furthermore, as AI capabilities advance rapidly, empirical assessments may systematically lag behind the capability frontier. Our framework provides a structured baseline for ongoing monitoring as capabilities advance.

title: A Thousand Faces: A Persuasion Benchmark with Experience-Grounded Persuadees Informed by Psychology and Pragmatics
summary: People can express the same beliefs and desires yet need different reasons to change their minds. What makes an argument relevant depends on how those views arose: experiences shape what a person finds credible, what matters to them, and what could prompt reconsideration. These personal grounds may also be expressed indirectly, through contextual clues in conversation. Benchmarks that specify beliefs and desires without these connections can reward arguments that match a description while overlooking whether they address the person's reasons. We introduce A Thousand Faces (ATF-Persu), with 1,000 personas across 200 topics and nine domains. Drawing on personality and attitude theories and conversational implicature, we construct five personas per factual context, linking experiences to judgments, expression, and grounds for revision. Evaluations show lower persuasion success than three comparison benchmarks under their respective protocols. Complete backgrounds yield broader use of supplied personal grounds and higher persona faithfulness than simplified specifications; blinded reviewers also rate ATF-Persu above CToMPersu on identifiable personal reasons, their influence on responses, and contextual expression. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Slandes/ATF-Persu.

Highlights

This release features 814 commits from 363 contributors (121 new)!

  • Structured decisions and generic parsers: the new POST /v1/systemone endpoint answers choice, noul and score questions over a structured state (#59299), is served by default (#60677, #60696), and also runs on Cloudflare/clef-omni (#61064), LiquidAI/d1-3B (#60676) and DiffusionGemma (#60466). The new hf tool and reasoning parser (--tool-call-parser hf, --reasoning-parser hf) reads the checkpoint's response_template, so models that ship it need no model-specific parser (#58604, #58602), in both the Python and Rust frontends (#59005).
  • Low-precision KV cache everywhere: NVFP4 KV cache now runs on SM8x and SM12x (#46963), SM90 (#60620) and with XQA decode on SM12x (#60452), and on MiniMax-M3 sparse attention on SM100 (#59300); GLM-5.x defaults to an FP8 KV cache on SM100, halving KV memory per rank with 2.3-5.5% more throughput at a 7-11% TTFT cost in the PR's benchmark (#60140, #60281); fp8_ds_mla on SM90 gives GLM-5.3-Flash up to 31% more output throughput (#59246); ROCm gains the 4-bit ultraquant_4bit KV cache with about 2x the density of FP8 (#57057).
  • Model Runner V2: a GPU n-gram speculator with variable-length drafts (#40704), Elastic EP (#53934), pipeline parallelism with prefill context parallelism for MLA models (#59139), a stock torch.compile mode (#59079), and MRV2 is now the default on ROCm with the model-specific MRV1 exceptions removed (#56360).
  • Faster startup and serving: vllm download-kernels installs FlashInfer's precompiled kernels (#58765); vllm preload --preload-autotune keeps the FlashInfer autotune table warm across restarts (#60085); a shared-memory tensor arena broadcasts large multimodal tensors to workers with one copy (#51207); tokenizers and processors load from the local snapshot (#60825); and with --api-server-count above 1 each connection goes to the least-loaded API worker, for 43-85% more req/s on short requests (Qwen3-0.6B, 32 input / 1 output tokens) in the PR's benchmark (#60723).
  • Model support: new EmbeddingGemma 2 omni-modal embeddings (#60254), MiniCPM-V 4.7 (#58674) and Nemotron 3.5 ASR (#59827); video input in the Transformers modeling backend (#57441); GLM-5.3 sparse MLA index conversions reused across layers (3.5-3.9x on that kernel, #59464) and fused multi-step draft decode (13.3% at concurrency 1, #57443); HiSparse per-request residency caching for up to 58% more throughput on GLM-5.3-NVFP4 on B200 with long, fully GPU-resident contexts at high concurrency (#60083).
  • Security: fixes for GHSA-4hhp-h66f-j5j7 (chat template resource exhaustion, #50300), GHSA-q97c-p368-75c4 (tokenizer max_token_id, #59491) and GHSA-frvg-qw88-hww9 (P2P ZMQ socket exhaustion, #51504); CORS no longer allows every origin by default (#61009); untrusted images are limited to raster formats (#60022); shared-memory multimodal cache handles are signed (#59357); and JSON schemas nested deeper than 64 levels are rejected (#60036).
  • Breaking changes: Python 3.10 dropped (#60402); default CORS origins restricted (#61009); transformers>=5.16.1,<5.20.0 and tokenizers>=0.23.2 (#57387, #59796); torch.compile sequence parallelism and AsyncTP passes removed (#60517); cascade attention removed (#61126); mamba_cache_mode="all" removed (#58997); max_tokens no longer reserved from the context window (#57035); Responses API reasoning stream events renamed (#59652).

Engine Core

  • Model Runner V2: GPU n-gram speculator (#40704), Elastic EP with drain-then-commit scaling (#53934), PP with PCP for MLA models (#59139), STOCK_TORCH_COMPILE mode (#59079), dynamic K in autoregressive speculators (#57053), MTP sampling-mask replay (#59359) and per-module LM heads (#58921), non-blocking H2D copies on WSL2 (#60215), and fixes for int64 index offsets at long context (#60736), warmup (#61013), GDN prefill checkpoints (#59536) and MRV2+PP+MTP align state (#60210).
  • Speculative decoding: fused multi-step draft decode on FlashInfer trtllm-gen (#58371), FlashInfer ReplaySSM for Mamba2 MTP (#52928), in-graph metadata for DFlash/DSpark drafts (#60692), and correctness fixes for ngram on hybrid recurrent models (#56531), Mamba prefill checkpoints with MTP and prefix caching (#59759, #60797), stop-string trimming (#47616), draft model config (#61240), adaptive block verification (#60945), DSpark bonus slots (#59105) and draft models on the Transformers backend (#59293).
  • Hybrid models and prefix caching: Mamba2 internal prefill checkpoints for NemotronH, Granite-4.0-H, Falcon-H1 and Zamba2 (#57329), stale block hashes dropped when streaming sessions truncate (#59103), and fixes for quantized Mamba-2 with TP (#58083), spec decode page sizes (#59975), prefix-cache bounds (#55601, #60533) and sm90 Mamba2 NaNs (#61718).
  • Sleep and RL: sleep releases workspace scratch (up to 4.5 GiB/GPU, #59156) and KV-init state (about 4.6 GiB/GPU, #59158), opt-in sleep_mode_offload_cudagraph (#59160, #59523); token-level weight-version spans on outputs (#59582, #61070); weight-transfer communicators released without stopping inference (#61060); --sleep-preserve-parameter-names 'draft.*' (#61046); modelexpress weight-transfer backend (#58399); POST /weight_checker (#51350); weight-transfer metrics (#55781); --enable-nccl-comm-suspend releasing the MNNVL workspace (#59360); and sleep(level=2) keeping FP8 KV scales (#57163).
  • HiSparse: per-request residency cache (up to 58% at high concurrency with GPU-resident contexts, #60083), lower scheduler overhead (#57930), GPU residency owned by HiSparse (#60647), less staging memory (#60429), host cache gauges (#58949, #59485), and fixes for decode token limits (#60682) and TP hangs (#60941).
  • Startup and memory: shared-memory tensor arena (--enable-shm-tensor-arena, on by default, #51207), Fast Start with PP (#55477), daemon-held weights counted against gpu_memory_utilization (#57298), autotune preload (#60085), local tokenizer snapshots (#60825), sparse_mla_prefill_workspace_factor saving several GiB at 1M context (#61023), cached memory reclaimed during weight loading (#57516), fewer Triton sampler warmup compiles (#58605), sharded state loader with PP (#52110), and reload_weights with Run:ai streamer (#58124).
  • Kernels and runtime: MoE weighted-sum tuning (1.17-2.37x, #59731), flash-maxsim kernels for ColBERT/ColPali scoring (#40337), fallback detokenization with 69% less CPU at 32K tokens (#60497), faster KV block free queue (#60269), Triton kernels off tl.make_block_ptr (#60502), fusion passes restored under PyTorch 2.15 (#57299) and static FP8 quant fusion on recent torch (#61108).
  • Batch invariance: custom all-reduce under VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 (#58623), deterministic split-K LoRA shrink (#59377), every attention backend checked (#60271), SM120 TP configs (#58495), and ROCm support (#52231).

Security

  • GHSA-4hhp-h66f-j5j7: chat templates are validated statically and rendered under a timeout (VLLM_CHAT_TEMPLATE_RENDER_TIMEOUT), user-supplied chat_template in Responses chat_template_kwargs is rejected, and the Rust frontend caps template execution (#50300).
  • GHSA-q97c-p368-75c4: tokenizer max_token_id off-by-one fixed (#59491).
  • GHSA-frvg-qw88-hww9: P2P ZMQ peer sessions are bounded by VLLM_P2P_MAX_PEERS (default 128), VLLM_P2P_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_S (default 30) and VLLM_P2P_IDLE_TIMEOUT_S (default 300), so unique peer addresses can no longer exhaust ZMQ sockets (#51504).
  • Default CORS settings no longer allow every origin in the Python and Rust frontends; set --allowed-origins to permit browser origins (#61009).
  • Untrusted images are opened with a raster-format allowlist (ALLOWED_IMAGE_FORMATS), denying EPS/PostScript and WMF (#60022); shared-memory multimodal cache handles are HMAC-signed and forged handles rejected (#59357).
  • Structured-output JSON schemas nested more than 64 levels return 400 (#60036); chunked /v1/embeddings requests keep cache_salt (#47696); Phi-4 MM audio no longer holds multi-GiB attention matrices (#60614); DeepSeek-OCR zero-sum pixel tensors no longer kill EngineCore (#59417).
  • Security dependency bumps: aiohttp>=3.14.3, pillow>=12.3.0, cryptography, urllib3, pyjwt and others (#59249, #59315, #59427).
