Build

  • Python 3.11-3.14 supported (#60402); macOS wheels built with the stable ABI (#60312); CUDA source builds require GCC 13 and fail early otherwise (#60259); Docker images compile Python bytecode at build time for faster container startup (#55422); VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED finds a compatible published wheel within the last 20 commits (#58871); the vendored DeepGEMM uses TORCH_LIBRARY (abi3, #48962).

Breaking Changes & Deprecations

  • Python 3.10 is no longer supported; the minimum is Python 3.11 (#60402).
  • Default CORS origins changed from * to none; set --allowed-origins for browser clients (#61009).
  • transformers>=5.16.1,<5.20.0 and tokenizers>=0.23.2 are required (#57387, #59796).
  • The torch.compile sequence parallelism and AsyncTP passes were removed, along with PassConfig.enable_sp, fuse_gemm_comms and sp_min_token_num; model-level sequence parallelism is unaffected (#60517).
  • Cascade attention was removed; --disable-cascade-attn still parses but only warns and will be removed in v0.33.0 (#61126).
  • mamba_cache_mode="all" was removed; --mamba-cache-mode all now fails validation (#58997).
  • Previously deprecated APIs were removed: wait_for_inflight_requests (use mode="wait"), AsyncLLM.pause_generation(), IOProcessor.output_to_response, vllm.scripts.main() and vllm bench throughput --dataset (#60923). The sonnet benchmark dataset was removed as scheduled (#60129). Tensorizer support was removed from LoRA (#60024), and the PyO3 vllm._rust_tool_parser bridge was removed (#59744).
  • API changes: max_tokens is treated as an upper bound on output rather than reserved from the context window (#57035); Responses API streaming uses response.content_part.added/done with part.type="reasoning_text" instead of response.reasoning_part.added/done (#59652); SamplingParams.prompt_logprob_token_ids is per row (#56984); /inference/v1/generate logprobs use integer token IDs (#58181); sleep API responses are standardized and invalid levels return 400 (#52864); return_mm_kwargs is deprecated in favor of mm_payload (#61427).
  • Watermarking: when the engine has watermarking configured, an omitted request field means enabled and only false opts out; unsupported combinations warn and fall back (#56801).
  • Rust frontend: qwen3_xml now parses Qwen3-Coder XML (alias of qwen3_coder); use the new qwen3_json for the JSON format (#60136).
  • New defaults: shared-memory tensor arena on (#51207); GLM-5.x FP8 KV cache on SM100 with --kv-cache-dtype auto (#60140, #60281); VLLM_DEEPEP_V2_ALLOW_HYBRID_MODE=1 (#57991); Humming preferred over Marlin on SM90 (#56997); sparse_mla_prefill_workspace_factor 2 above 256K max_model_len (#61023); MRV2 on ROCm with model-specific MRV1 exceptions removed (#56360); VLLM_ROCM_AITER_MLA_DCP_VERIFY=auto (#59965); dtype=auto picks bfloat16 on PowerPC (#58528); MXFP4 W4A4 checkpoints fall back to W4A16 with a warning when no W4A4 kernel exists (#60079).
  • Stricter validation: incompatible --prefix-match-unit (#58021), max_num_scheduled_tokens=0 (#60714), HiSparse with cudagraph_mode=FULL (#59688), and negative --device-ids (#49053) are rejected at startup.

title: PLANE: Plug-and-Play Fine-Grained Visual Experts for Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) commonly suffer from hallucinations, which appear as fabricating non-existent objects or outputting incorrect attributes and spatial relationships in images. Previous works empirically indicate that CLIP-style vision encoders tend to focus on primary objects while ignoring image details, which is one of the causes of hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose plug-and-play fine-grained visual experts (PLANE) comprising two components: LoRA visual experts operating on CLIP for multi-aspect image encoding, and an instruction-aware gate network for adaptive image feature fusion. During training, we construct a fine-grained image-caption pairs dataset, where images are described from three aspects: objects, attributes, and relations between objects. Image-caption pairs from different aspects are used to train the three fine-grained LoRA experts respectively. Aiming at comprehensively evaluate our method's capabilities, we manually annotate a fine-grained hallucination evaluation benchmark for LVLMs which is GPT4-independent during evaluation phase (GIFT). We conduct experiments both on popular hallucination evaluation benchmarks and GIFT. The results show that our method effectively reduces hallucinations across models of different types and sizes while introducing minimal inference latency. Compared to advanced baselines, our model also demonstrates superior performance.

title: TIRE: Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution for Physics Problem Synthesis
summary: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. LLM-based synthesis from texts scales efficiently, but model-generated answers and assessments leave supervision vulnerable to hallucinations. We introduce TIRE, a framework for Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution that brings knowledge-driven problem construction to large-scale data generation. Top-down instantiation uses reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions to control the physical relations and numerical configurations of generated problems. Reliable execution establishes reference answers before problem generation, providing a common numerical foundation for problem construction and teacher distillation. Together, these mechanisms combine control over problem content with execution-grounded supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Using TIRE, we construct TIRE-19k, spanning nine subfields of physics. Across 3 backbone LLMs and 4 benchmarks, TIRE-19k outperforms 5 representative datasets with equal amounts of SFT data, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.86 percentage points on average. Further GRPO raises Qwen3-8B's average accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint. These results demonstrate the value of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge with reliable execution.

title: Beyond Factual Accuracy: A Benchmark for Evaluating Perspective Alignment in LLMs
summary: Large Language Models often generate factually correct responses that fail to maintain user-requested perspectives, blending multiple perspectives and forcing users to filter through unwanted information---a perspective control failure that factual accuracy metrics cannot detect. We introduce PerspectiveBench, a benchmark quantifying perspective alignment by constructing scenarios where multiple valid reasoning paths coexist, and propose the Perspective Alignment Score (PAS) to measure adherence to specified perspectives. Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art models successfully include target content but fail to exclude non-requested perspectives. Providing documents through RAG improves factual grounding but does not resolve perspective drift, as models prioritize comprehensive coverage over strict user constraints. Code and data are available at https://github.com/sunghoon014/PerspectiveBench.

title: Revealing what benchmark scores hide: Jointly measuring the breadth and reliability of LLM capabilities using accessibility profiles
summary: Language model benchmarks assign each question a single outcome from one fixed wording, even though the same underlying request can be expressed in many equivalent ways. We argue that the quantity of interest should therefore not be correctness on one wording, but the accessibility of an inquiry, which we define as the probability that a model succeeds across meaning-preserving formulations. The distribution of accessibility across inquiries reveals a structure that accuracy and existing best-, worst-, or average-case prompt scores collapse: how broadly a model's capabilities extend across inquiries and how dependably those capabilities can be elicited. Two models can have the same average performance while one succeeds across more inquiries unreliably and the other succeeds across fewer inquiries but more consistently, leading to opposite preferences depending on whether the task allows multiple retries until one success or when repeated consistent success is required. Across six benchmarks and more than twenty models, this tradeoff is common: for about half of the model pairs with nearly equal mean accessibility, which model looks better depends on whether one success across five formulations is enough or all five must succeed, quantities we call Access@5 and Reliable@5, respectively. For some pairs the two measures diverge significantly, by up to 10 points in opposite directions. Accessibility also reveals that scaling, reasoning, and prompt optimization can redistribute capability across inquiries in ways aggregate accuracy obscures, sometimes broadening the set of inquiries a model can succeed on while making success on them less repeatable. Accessibility turns formulation sensitivity from a nuisance into a measurable property of capability, distinguishing what a model can sometimes succeed on from what users can actually depend on.

title: TrustAgent-RFF: Agentic Diagnostic Planning for Reliable RF Fingerprinting under Domain Shift
summary: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.

title: A Cross-Domain Evaluation of Prompting Techniques for Large Language Models
summary: Prompt engineering has become a central mechanism for guiding the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a wide range of reasoning and language understanding tasks [1], [2]. However, existing studies frequently evaluate prompting techniques using different LLMs, datasets, or task settings, making direct comparisons across methods and domains difficult [3]. Consequently, in this paper we present a controlled cross-domain evaluation of Zero-Shot prompting, Few-Shot prompting, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and automatic prompt optimization based on a PE2-inspired optimization pipeline [4]-[6]. All experiments were conducted with the same LLM and evaluated on six benchmark datasets covering arithmetic reasoning, logical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and factual verification. The results show that no prompting strategy consistently outperforms the others across all domains, and pairwise statistical comparisons of the highest-performing configurations revealed no significant differences. RAG achieves the highest overall average accuracy of 78.33% when 300 examples are available for retrieval, while Few-Shot Prompting achieves comparatively high accuracies across several structured reasoning tasks. Zero-Shot Prompting remains competitive on tasks with self-contained inputs, whereas the PE2-inspired optimization approach produces stable but not systematically superior results compared to the other evaluated prompting techniques. Furthermore, increasing the number of task-specific examples does not consistently improve performance across prompting techniques, indicating strong domain and task dependency. These findings suggest that prompting techniques should be selected adaptively based on task characteristics rather than treated as universally applicable optimization strategies.

title: MisleadQA: Diagnosing LLM Failures under Misleading Context
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer questions from retrieved or user-provided context. However, provided context can be factually true yet out-of-scope, describing a different entity, time, or location from the one the question targets, and still lead models to a wrong answer. Prior work has mainly studied factually false or irrelevant context. It remains unclear whether such out-of-scope context misleads models as much as false context, and whether adding gold context prevents models from being misled by either. We introduce **MisleadQA**, a diagnostic dataset of multiple-choice questions with an abstention option. Each question pairs gold context (G) with true but out-of-scope context (S) and false but in-scope context (F) supporting the same wrong answer. We evaluate six open-weight LLMs. On questions they answer correctly without context, providing S alone leads them to switch to this wrong answer in 29.3% of cases, and providing F alone does so in 75.4%. Adding G nearly removes the effect of S, but F still misleads models in 21.0% of cases, especially when F comes first. A context-faithful instruction reduces these errors mainly through abstention and lowers accuracy even with G. These findings suggest that evaluations should check whether context applies to the question, not only whether it is true, and should report correct, misled, and abstention rates together. Data and code are available at [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA).

title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
summary: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. We introduce a risk-sensitive evaluation framework that scores responses by the presence and severity of six categories of risk-bearing language (treatment directives, contraindications, dosage expressions, urgency-triage cues, high-alert medication mentions, and overconfident assertions), anchored on published clinical harm taxonomies. Severity is classified by a three-judge LLM ensemble. We apply this framework to six 7-9B instruction-tuned models, three general (Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3.1-8B) and three medically adapted (BioMistral-7B, OpenBioLLM-Llama3-8B, Med42-Llama3-8B), on 200 real patient questions from the K-QA benchmark. Two findings emerge. First, ensemble risk-bearing language is statistically independent of factual hallucination rate (pooled Spearman $ρ= -0.065$, $n = 300$, 95% CI $[-0.18, +0.05]$; distance correlation $= 0.10$, independence test $p = 0.24$). Second, medical fine-tuning does not reduce aggregate risk but reshapes it: continued-pretraining adaptations (BioMistral, OpenBioLLM) consistently suppress high-alert medication mentions while amplifying overconfident assertions, whereas clinical instruction-tuning (Med42) suppresses dosing only, without amplifying overconfidence. Per-category Krippendorff $α$ is fair to good for the four linguistically anchored categories (0.53-0.71) and low for the two clinical-judgment-dependent categories (0.19, 0.31), indicating where automatic safety evaluation is and is not yet reliable. We release the rubric, judge prompts, and evaluation code.

title: Where Natural Language Ends in Agents: Executable Skill Composition with MetaSkill
summary: Agent Skills express open-ended task knowledge in natural language, but composing them requires persistent execution order and upstream-output handoffs. We propose selective formalization at Skill boundaries: coordination relations with stable references and machine-checkable constraints become executable, while substantive task judgments remain within Skills. We introduce MetaSkill, a hybrid representation that preserves complete Skill packages and local instructions while making invocation dependencies and predecessor-text bindings executable through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) runtime. This interface supports explicit coordination without prescribing how each Skill performs its local task. Across 20 multi-Skill artifact tasks and two LLMs, we compare natural-language procedures, prompt-visible graphs, and MetaSkill derived from a common frozen plan per task, using the same designated Skill packages. Additional comparisons evaluate AgentSkillOS with the same available Skill packages as MetaSkill, as well as agent systems using their configured tools. Blinded artifact judgments yield favorable preference point estimates across all reported comparisons, with 95% task-bootstrap intervals excluding parity against Prompt Graph under DeepSeek-V4-Flash and OpenClaw under GLM-5.2. In audited GLM-5.2 execution traces, all planned nodes complete and all declared precedence constraints are satisfied. Together, these findings support MetaSkill as a practical interface for composing open-ended Skills, combining local linguistic flexibility with executable dependencies, explicit predecessor-text bindings, and auditable coordination. Code is available at: https://github.com/TokenRhythm/opensquilla/tree/paper/metaskill-lp4fm-2026

title: Neuro-Inspired Inhibitory Message Passing for Accurate and Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning
summary: Multi-agent systems promise to solve problems by bringing together information beyond the reach of any individual agent. Retrieval and tool use can distribute this information across agents, making communication essential to collaboration. A central challenge is keeping crucial evidence visible in each agent's context as messages accumulate. Repeated information can crowd out rare, decisive evidence. Models of cortical circuits suggest a principle for addressing this imbalance: inhibition can selectively suppress shared inputs while preserving sensitivity to weaker signals. We adapt this principle into inhibitory message passing, a training-free communication router that cancels redundant evidence separately for each evidence sentence and receiver. Each round, it forwards evidence sentences restated in agents' messages, delivering each at most once to receivers whose own evidence lacks it and excluding the senders' reasoning and answers. Against standard message passing, accuracy in peer groups rose by 39-77 percentage points across three benchmarks, and tokens per run fell by 10-46%. Gains held across seven open models spanning four to thirty-two billion parameters and two commercial models, in groups up to sixty-four agents, and across multi-agent architectures including peer-to-peer, orchestrator-worker, and multilevel hierarchical organizations. These findings support a scalable design pattern for more accurate and token-efficient multi-agent reasoning.

title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
summary: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface. The benchmark spans progressively larger program scopes, from individual operators to compact model graphs, across representative edge application domains. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.

title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
summary: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
summary: Software quality has long rested on specifications that state what code must do, and on testing and verification that check that the code does it. Agentic systems change this foundation: they replace parts of their logic, such as choosing the next tool, judging whether an action is allowed, or writing code to run, with calls to a large language model (LLM). The program still relies on what this logic must guarantee, but the model's behavior is not fixed by code, varies across runs, and can be steered by its input. The guarantee must therefore come from the program around each LLM call site, as a contract of pre-conditions, prompt constraints, and post-conditions. We present an empirical study of these contracts in 496 LLM call sites of 40 popular open-source agentic systems (13.4 MLOC, four languages). Using a multi-agent pipeline validated by 17,428 human judgments, we trace where every model output flows, derive an expected contract for each call site without access to its code, and compare it with the contract that the code implements. We find that 48% of LLM outputs reach control flow or execution, and 73% of these never reach a person. Programs enforce 78% of their constraints in code, but in the prompt, 67% of the constraints are only requested from the model. Although 82% of call sites are checked before and after the call, 63% of the expected constraints are unmet and only 5.3% of call sites satisfy their whole contract; ten recurring patterns explain 99% of the gaps. 38 mechanisms behind these gaps trigger at runtime, and a small code fix that enforces the expected constraint stops all 38. Our results show that the presence of checks says little about their adequacy, and we derive implications for agent developers, framework maintainers, and researchers.

title: IF-MAP: Influence-Function-Inspired Agent Prioritization in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Improving every agent in an LLM-based multi-agent system can be prohibitively costly, making it important to identify which agent should be prioritized to achieve the greatest system-level gain with limited resources. Failure attribution can inform this decision, but an agent's responsibility for failures does not directly reveal the system-level gains achievable by improving it. We therefore introduce IF-MAP, an influence-function-inspired method for identifying agents with high potential for system-level improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP measures end-to-end loss changes under controlled semantic prompt perturbations, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace, and uses the estimated response norm as a priority score. This black-box procedure requires no access to model parameters or gradients and produces agent priorities that can guide subsequent improvement effort. We evaluate IF-MAP across six multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, using the same priorities for prompt optimization and model upgrades. Optimizing the selected agents' prompts achieves a macro-average gain of 3.81 percentage points, compared with 1.85 for uniform agent selection. Across five target models, upgrading the selected agents yields macro-average gains of 7.62-16.42 percentage points, compared with 3.81-8.62 for uniform agent selection. Despite its probing overhead, IF-MAP reduces Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V3.2 token use by 74.2% and 35.2%, respectively, relative to optimizing every agent, and reduces target-model tokens by 63.6-64.9% relative to upgrading every agent. These results support the use of IF-MAP to identify promising agents and direct improvement effort toward greater end-to-end performance gains.

title: Is This Your Agent? Identity Watermarking for Agent Systems in Dynamic Environments
summary: Agent systems deployed in dynamic environments continuously update their memories, skills, and runtime configurations, leading to evolving trajectories and challenges for persistent identity authentication. Existing text and agent watermarking methods struggle to achieve stable watermark embedding under dynamic environments, while embedded watermarks may become difficult to recover due to environmental changes. This paper proposes DASMark, an identity watermarking framework for dynamic agent systems. DASMark introduces Action-Preserving Embedding (APE), which learns semantically similar but distinguishable decision-expression channels from diverse interaction trajectories to enable stable watermark embedding in dynamic systems. It further introduces Shift-Robust Recovery (SRR) to mitigate context-induced shifts and improve watermark recovery stability under dynamic environments. In dynamic settings, DASMark achieves 98.5% bit-decoding accuracy and maintains 95.2% accuracy under attack scenarios, while preserving task utility comparable to unwatermarked agents.

title: Train Locally, Learn Together: Distributed Multi-Agent Training via ADMM
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can outperform individual language-model agents by combining specialized roles, diverse reasoning processes, and collaborative decision-making. However, collaborative MAS training is typically centralized, requiring a common trainer to aggregate role-local trajectories and learning signals and maintain model and optimization states. This motivates a distributed multi-agent learning paradigm in which agents improve system-level capabilities through role-local learning and decentralized communication, paving the way toward scalable, resilient, and self-organizing MAS. To this end, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first optimization-grounded framework for distributed MAS training based on consensus alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). We formulate collaborative MAS learning as a consensus-constrained finite-sum optimization problem, naturally lending itself to distributed optimization via ADMM. The proposed approach alternates role-local learning with inter-agent consensus using distributed communication protocols such as ring all-reduce, enabling joint optimization while keeping each agent's data and training state local. We evaluate our framework on distributed safety alignment and general reasoning tasks. Under compromised-agent settings, ADMM can reduce HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) by up to 26.4%, while achieving reasoning gains comparable to centralized training. These results show that distributed MAS training retains the benefits of centralized joint optimization without requiring a centralized trainer.

title: Measuring the Task Value of Precision Upgrades in Closed-Loop Agents
summary: A low-precision agent can call its full-precision (BF16) model at selected decisions as a fallback. A learned precision router chooses where to call it from the disagreement between the two models and is judged by end-to-end success. An inserted BF16 action, however, can rescue a failing task or damage a succeeding one. We argue that a fallback's value is the number of tasks it saves minus the number it spoils, measured for the intervention that will actually run. From restored states, we run paired branches that cross which model supplies the current action with which model continues, separating replacement of one action, takeover of later execution, and both. On Qwen3 agents with simulated 4-bit weights in tau2-bench, replacing the first action where the two models differed in tool use changed many task outcomes, but rescues and damages nearly cancelled, and on held-out telecom tasks the action-only estimate was negative. Replacing both the action and the continuation had a positive net gain in two of five exploratory lower-bit stress settings. Two references changed outcomes at fixed bit width: replacing an action with that of a second 4-bit checkpoint changed about as many outcomes as replacing it with the BF16 action, and reordering tool-argument keys changed outcomes while the executed tool call stayed identical. At common states, the additional value of the BF16 action over that checkpoint remained unresolved. A frozen uncertainty trigger found more outcome changes than random selection, while its net benefit stayed within the range of random selection. We recommend evaluating each fallback by its signed task benefit under the intended continuation, against same-precision references, before attributing gains to more bits.

title: VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations Research
summary: Advances in reasoning, coding, and tool use enable LLM agents to solve operations research (OR) problems through iterative problem modeling, program construction, and verification. Yet passing self-authored verification does not ensure that the solutions satisfy task constraints and meet optimization quality. This gap can arise from correlated specification errors, where the generated program and its checks share omissions or misinterpretations of task requirements, alongside incomplete verification coverage and ineffective optimization strategies. We propose VERAS, a verification-guided adaptive search harness for reliable OR that uses verification evidence to prioritize feasibility repair, constraint-coverage review, and solution-quality improvement. VERAS combines task-specific solution checkers with a separate verification agent to examine candidate solutions against the task requirements. It uses verification feedback to guide feasibility repair, additional constraint checking, and objective improvement, while candidate acceptance criteria screen revisions for deterioration in output validity or constraint satisfaction. On ORAgentBench, VERAS achieves a 42.99% pass rate, exceeding the reported 35.51% of Codex using the same LLM. Across two industrial-scale OR problems, VERAS reduces inter-datacenter peak bandwidth by 10.34% relative to native Codex and lowers annualized distribution network planning costs by 6.28% compared with expert-designed solutions. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/holimario/VERAS.

title: CME-SpectrumBench: Can LLMs Analyze Condensed Matter Spectral Data?
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are presently well assessed by expert-level mathematics and physics benchmarks which focus on theoretical, symbolic reasoning. However, we lack experimental benchmarks that evaluate data analysis in frontier research problems, a capability that future domain-specific foundation models must have. To this end, we present CME-SpectrumBench, an expert-designed benchmark consisting of 190 questions that measures how reliably frontier LLMs analyze research-level spectral scientific data in condensed matter experiments (CME). Using simulated CME spectral data, we prompt models to identify structures from 2D intensity arrays in the face of noise and limited instrumental resolution, a test of dense context reasoning. Models are scored by how accurately their numerical answers approach the ground truth. Under direct query, scores generally pale in comparison to handwritten code due to clear failure modes: models can find simple features but struggle to trace patterns or compute derived quantities, and performance typically degrades with increased data resolution and noise/convolution levels. LLM performance becomes comparable to handwritten code by allowing tool use (access to a Python interpreter) with/without ReAct prompting, in effect mapping questions onto agentic code generation problems. Our findings show that frontier models can serve as research assistants by interfacing with data through code, but still face difficulties processing information directly from large datasets - a key barrier future foundation models must overcome. The code and data are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/jingene/CMESpectrumBench.

title: Not Every User Says It All: Training Tool-Using Agents Beyond Ideal Simulated Users
summary: Tool-using agents are trained and evaluated almost exclusively with strong simulated users who state every detail clearly, yet real users are often weaker. We construct weak users by masking sentences of a simulated user's replies, holding the task and the user's knowledge fixed, and cross-evaluate agents trained with strong and weak users on tau2-bench and ToolWOZ. Weak users lower the success of every policy, and training with them does not help: no policy trained with weak users, through fixed masks, mixtures or a curriculum, serves weak users better than the strong-trained policy beyond run-to-run noise, and prompting the agent to ask more does not help either. We propose StaGPO (State-Grouped Policy Optimization): the agent writes what the task needs, what is missing and how it is being filled, and GRPO uses this state to compare turns of different rollouts that reach the same situation, assigning step-level credit. Within the standard recipe of a small SFT cold start followed by RL, StaGPO makes weak-user training useful: on ToolWOZ, the Qwen3.5-2B policy trained with weak users reaches 76.8% with weak users, the highest of any Qwen3.5-2B policy we trained, 4.8 points above GRPO and 2.8 above the strongest baseline; it is also 5.4 points above GRPO with strong users, and generalises to an unseen mask rate; trained with strong users instead, it serves weak users at least as well as GRPO trained with weak users. On tau2-bench it scores highest with weak users for both models, by a small margin for Qwen3.5-4B.

title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
summary:
We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"

Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

— Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang, How the Claude Code team does code review

title: Agents' Last Doubt: Knowing When to Act and When to Step Back in Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents repeatedly face decision points under uncertainty, choosing between autonomous action, additional information gathering, and human escalation. These decisions require balancing task success against interaction cost and the risk of irreversible errors. Learning to make these trade-offs is challenging because existing interaction trajectories record only the outcomes of actions taken, leaving the consequences of alternative actions unobserved. To address this gap, we construct a counterfactual dataset containing 3,115 action outcomes from 1,036 decision points in ToolSandbox. At each decision point, we execute each legal action and evaluate its downstream outcomes based on task completion, interaction cost, and irreversible errors. Using this dataset, we train SURE-Act, a controller that selects actions for a frozen backbone agent at inference time. Our experiments show that learning to rank alternative actions improves offline action-selection utility by 0.0309 over a regression-only baseline. We further show that adding SURE-Act enables end-to-end gains of up to 0.0575 in ToolSandbox's Overall Score with the Qwen3-4B agent. Moreover, SURE-Act outperforms adapted decision rules from SAGE-Agent and Calibrate-Then-Act by 0.1506 and 0.1438, respectively. This work establishes the first counterfactual dataset for ToolSandbox and provides actionable insights into decision-making under uncertainty for tool-using agents.

title: Does AI-Assisted Development Homogenize Software? An Empirical Study of Code Similarity, Quality, and Evolution
summary: AI-assisted software development is evolving from interactive LLM assistance toward agentic systems that autonomously perform software engineering tasks, yet the effects of this shift remain insufficiently understood. We present an empirical study of 50 long-lived Java and Python open-source projects across three eras: pre-LLM, potentially LLM-assisted, and detected agentic development. Using snapshots from Software Heritage, we examine code similarity, software quality, and software evolution. Similarity is measured semantically through embedding-based cosine similarity and syntactically through CodeBLEU*. Quality is assessed with SonarQube metrics covering maintainability, complexity, reliability, and security. Evolution is characterized by annualized growth rates of LOC, functions, classes, files, and statements, and by commit activity in the three months preceding each snapshot. Results show no consistent evidence of increased similarity as semantic and syntactic similarity decreased significantly in Java for both the LLM and agentic eras relative to the pre-LLM era, while Python showed no significant differences. Software quality remained largely stable, although the agentic era showed significantly lower code-smell and SQALE index densities. Structural growth was generally lower in the agentic era, particularly for files, whereas development activity increased moderately in Java, especially in commits and added lines. These findings challenge the assumption that LLM- and agent-assisted development necessarily homogenizes code, degrades quality, or accelerates growth.

title: DrugHarness: An Evolvable Agent Harness for Computational Drug Discovery
summary: Computational drug discovery requires agents to compose scientific operations and adapt to changing evidence and constraints. Here we introduce DrugHarness, an evolvable agent harness coupling composable scientific execution with conditional skill induction. Its environment integrates over 80 scientific operations, biomedical resources and task-specific code, preserving associations among candidates, results and artifacts. From execution trajectories and outcome feedback, DrugHarness induces action hypotheses with observable applicability conditions, recommended actions and supporting evidence. An independent review agent evaluates candidate skills derived from these hypotheses through source verification and, when needed, targeted execution trials. Admitted skills guide subsequent tasks and are revised through feedback. Evaluation on MolBench and SMDD-Bench demonstrates capabilities in molecular screening, optimization and constrained design. Without evolution, DrugHarness exceeds reported MolClaw-CC results by 10.8 percentage points in affinity-comparison accuracy and 55% in mean top-three active hits on MolBench. Retrospective evaluation on skill-development tasks shows that evolution increases Qwen's affinity-comparison accuracy from 62.2% to 81.1% and optimization success from 79.5% to 87.2%. In a prospective HPK1 study, DrugHarness achieves a more favorable median docking score than Biomni among system-specific candidates. A synthesized compound achieves a cellular IC50 of 14.19 nM, a 2.64-fold potency improvement over the best input reference, with activity competitive with two selected compounds designed by experienced medicinal chemists. These results support conditional skill evolution for scientific agents and demonstrate a workflow connecting computational drug design with experimental validation.

title: ToolRosetta: Surface-Form Invariance of Tool-Call Guards
summary: Step-level guards for tool-using agents are evaluated on tidy JSON tool calls, but deployed coding agents act through execute_bash and execute_code tools whose payloads are strings. We introduce ToolRosetta, which re-renders every candidate action in the AgentDojo and AgentHarm splits of TS-Bench as a Python call, as a shell command, and without the agent's rationale. The renderings are produced by code and verified by round-trip parsing, so the user request, the history, the label and the action's effect stay fixed while only the surface form changes. Across eleven guards with two placebo controls, frontier and strong open-weight guards are stable: no frontier error rate moves by more than 3.4 points. Four of five specialized agent guards are not: under the shell form their false-positive rates rise by 21 to 47 points on AgentDojo, and TS-Guard's by 38 points on its own home benchmark, blocking between a third and nine in ten benign actions; the fifth, StepGuard, does not move. A small open guard drifts five points more permissive. Removing the agent's rationale moves most guards whose input carries it, in guard-specific directions. A request-blind control on one guard shows that the rationale is where intent is read from. A parser that restores the canonical call in front of the guard removes the effect for these renderings, by construction. Benchmark accuracy on JSON calls does not predict a guard's operating point behind a code-acting agent.

title: GLOBE: Evolving Structured Agentic Memory for E-commerce Product Optimization in Generative Search
summary: Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.

title: Architecting autonomy: A design pattern for high-compute, governed agents in biotech
summary:
In production systems today, most AI agents operate as lightweight dispatchers. They parse a prompt, make an API call, retrieve a record, and hand back control. Their execution is fast, stateless and cheap. Biotechnology does not work this way. 

Folding a protein target, screening a 50,000 compound ligand library, or evaluating structure-activity relationships (SAR) are not quick API lookups. They are sustained, stateful, GPU-bound simulations that run for minutes or even hours across specialized silicon. When you ask a general-purpose large language model (LLM) endpoint to coordinate a complex drug discovery workflow, the standard paradigm breaks: Timeouts occur, context windows overflow with atomic coordinates, and proprietary chemical Intellectual Property (IP) risks exposure to external networks. 

Building enterprise grade research and development (R&D) agents requires moving past the monolithic assistant model. In this blog post, we will discuss how to use a three-layer architecture: separating cognitive orchestration (the brain) from computational execution (the muscle), and anchoring both inside an enterprise governance plane to build scalable agents for drug discovery use cases in biotech.

A three-layer pattern

The reference architecture below shows how to architect, optimize, and govern high-compute autonomous agents in biotechnology, specifically Drug Discovery.

The execution layer: scaling the muscle - high-compute execution 

The execution layer is responsible for the heavy scientific computations. The first architectural decision is determining where workloads should run:

  • Strategic, proprietary pipelines require dedicated GPU infrastructure within your security perimeter

  • Routine or standardized workloads can safely be delegated to managed cloud endpoints

In this architecture, protein folding is driven by ESMFold and generative design by GenMol. Both run as NVIDIA Inference Microservices or NIMs deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using G4 VMs backed by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

A critical hurdle in containerized GPU workloads is the cold-start penalty, the latency delay required to pull multi-gigabyte model weights from an image registry and stage them into GPU memory (VRAM).

To ensure low latency responsiveness, we build the following as a recommendation into the reference architecture:

  • Maintain warm pools: Pin the GKE node pool to a minimum of one active node.

  • Preload weights: Model weights are loaded directly into VRAM at pod initialization, ensuring containers are immediately ready for inference.

  • Resilient scheduling: GKE manages pod lifecycles and restarts failed instances without tearing down the underlying VM infrastructure. 

This approach trades custom, manual CUDA kernel tuning for NVIDIA's pre-compiled, containerized runtimes, dramatically reducing infrastructure engineering overhead while ensuring deterministic throughput.

In biotech, chemical structures represent millions of dollars in proprietary IP. A docking request transmits SMILE strings or 3D coordinate matrices that must never leave company custody.

Containerized NIMs eliminate the friction between rapid prototyping and rigorous data isolation. During early exploration, researchers can query NVIDIA hosted endpoints. When transitioning to proprietary lead candidates, the exact same container is deployed to GKE inside a private VPC. The agent’s orchestration logic remains identical; only the target URI updates from an external proxy to an internal VPC endpoint. No structural data leaves the enterprise perimeter.

The cognitive layer: Multi-agent reasoning

With compute execution isolated, the cognitive layer manages agentic workflow sequencing. Built on Agent Runtime, within the Gemini platform, this reference architecture shows a system that deploys a hierarchical multi-agent structure, one lead orchestrator, and two specialized domain sub-agents (Lead Optimization and Safety Screening) . The multi-agent design can be modified to suit the use case at hand. 

Based on this design, when an end-user submits a high-level task such as “ Analyze Candidate 4b against Target X and produce a SAR report”, the system applies four core orchestration patterns discussed below; 

  • In-process native agent handoffs: The lead orchestrator delegates tasks to specialist sub-agents using Agent Runtime’s native SDK rather than network-serialized agent-to-agent HTTP protocols. This eliminates intermediate network hops and keeps internal handoffs instantaneous. Only the outermost boundary communicates outward to user-facing surfaces like the Gemini agent.
  • Passing bulky payloads by reference: LLMs degrade quickly when forced to ingest massive arrays of 3D spatial coordinates. In this architecture, raw structural data (PDB files, docking poses, trajectory logs) is written directly to Cloud Storage. Agents pass lightweight, signed object URIs and high-level structural summaries, keeping context windows compact and inference costs down.
  • Decoupling workflow logic from biochemical reasoning: General-purpose LLMs excel at task planning and synthesis, but are prone to hallucinating biochemical nuances. To control this behavior, this architecture maintains strong separation of concerns, namely, workflow and tasks decomposition are handled by Gemini. Domain chemistry and pharmacological reasoning are handled by specialized Nemotron models hosted on dedicated GPU nodes. 
  • Context-driven evaluation over rigid cutoffs: Traditional computational screening enforces arbitrary numerical cutoffs (e.g., discard if binding affinity ,-7.5 kcal/mol) However, therapeutic context fundamentally alters risk tolerance. Preventive cardiovascular therapy taken daily by healthy patients requires extremely strict safety margins, or a novel oncology candidate targeting an intractable cancer may accept higher toxicity if efficacy is demonstrated.

By passing disease context directly into the specialized reasoning models, drug candidates are evaluated against dynamic, target-specific profiles rather than static thresholds, preventing the premature culling of viable drug leads.

Performance best practices for high-compute pipelines

Optimizing an agentic system that interfaces with heavy GPU compute requires challenging common engineering instincts:

Common Assumption

Architectural Reality

Recommended Best Practice

"Swap in a faster driver model to cut latency."

The primary orchestrator's token generation is rarely the bottleneck in multi-step R&D pipelines.

Optimize I/O, not token speed: Focus on reducing payload sizes and intermediate network hops rather than compromising orchestrator reasoning depth.

"Parallelize tool calls across workers."

External scientific services and containerized models often serialize requests internally on dedicated hardware.

Respect execution topology: Align client-side concurrency with backend queue mechanics to prevent pipeline lockouts and connection timeouts.

"Pass full simulation states between tools."

Large JSON bodies cause schema validation failures, prompt truncation, and token bloat.

Pass heavy payloads by reference: Store raw coordinates in object storage and pass lightweight URIs between agent boundaries.

"Return outputs only when the pipeline finishes."

Long multi-minute runs leave scientists blind to whether jobs are proceeding or stalled.

Stream intermediate stage completions: Emit progress updates at each completed milestone (e.g., folding complete, docking running) for real-time visibility.

"Chain multiple granular micro-tools."

Deep tool-chains increase the probability of hallucinated arguments and schema mismatches.

Collapse compute pipelines: Wrap end-to-end simulation pipelines behind a single, clean tool interface that takes clear parameters and returns a consolidated object.

The enterprise governance and asymmetric autonomy

Deploying high-compute agents in enterprise environments requires robust data sovereignty, audit trails, and process control. The Gemini platform establishes these safeguards natively with the following components: 

  • Agent Identity: Every autonomous agent operates with a cryptographically verifiable identity. Thus, for a biotech use case, when a candidate molecule is advanced or rejected, the event is permanently logged to that specific agent principal. 

  • Agent Gateway: This serves the single ingress/egress point for every interaction within the perimeter. Centralized IAM and regional residency rules help ensure sensitive molecular data remains within designated cloud regions. 

  • Agent Registry: This feature maintains a curated catalog of approved agents, validated tool schemas, and authorized Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, preventing rogue tools from executing in production. 

  • Model Armor: This functionality inspects incoming prompts and outgoing payloads in real time to prevent prompt injection and data exfiltration. 

The payoff is clear. Identity, RBAC, auditing, residency, and data protection are native properties of the Gemini platform; this allows enterprise customers to focus on science rather than having to build a compliance stack for every project. 

In high-stakes research and development, full autonomy introduces unacceptable liability, while requiring approval for trivial steps can create frictions. The solution addressing this to use asymmetric gating in the following ways;

Automate reversible operations: For example, allow the agent to resolve chemical naming synonyms, pull structural PDBs, and run preliminary Lipinski screens autonomously without interrupting the researcher.

Gate irreversible operations: For instance, initiating multi-GPU docking run, advancing a lead compound to wet-lab synthesis, or archiving a therapeutic program must require explicit human sign-off.

The pattern, and the path forward

High-compute autonomous agents succeed when the boundaries between cognitive planning, numerical computation, and system governance are clean in the following ways:

  1. Keep the orchestrator focused on decomposition and synthesis, leaving intensive biophysical simulation to specialized, containerized microservices and models.

  2. Eliminate context bloat by passing complex chemical data by reference through cloud storage.

  3. Anchor the workflow in enterprise governance, pairing cryptographic agent identity with asymmetric human oversight.

As generative and structural biology models expand toward whole-cell modeling and complex dynamic simulations, this decoupled architecture ensures research systems scale efficiently while keeping proprietary IP secure and auditable.

title: Four evaluation engineering lessons learned from building agent plugins
summary:
The real challenge of building an agentic system isn't the construction, it's the measurement. 

Evaluation engineering is a critical foundation for building reliable AI systems. Setting up systematic, repeatable tests to measure your agent’s true behavior can be the difference between shipping a tool you can trust and one that silently breaks, fails to call APIs, or makes mistakes. 

I’ve run evaluation engineering initiatives for years at Google and developing the newly released Google Cloud Developer plugin served as a live testbed to stress-test these key principles across real-world developer workflows.

Here are four eval lessons we learned from building the new plugin that you can apply to your own builds.

1. Grade the execution steps instead of the summary

When we first evaluated agents, we set up an LLM-as-judge to inspect the agent’s final text reply and scored it against a checklist. However, we quickly realized it’s fundamentally flawed because the grader only sees what the agent wrote, not what it actually did. When we ran our initial 11-prompt evaluation suite for the Google Cloud Developer plugin, the automated grader marked it as failing three prompts. But when we opened the raw tool-call logs and read the transcripts, the plugin had actually passed all three. On a Cloud Run cleanup prompt, for instance, our rubric required checking command syntax before running anything. The agent ran gcloud help run services list as its very first step. It did the work, but its final message was focused on warning the user about permanent data loss rather than reciting that it had checked the help docs.

The grader penalized the agent for doing the right thing simply because it didn’t brag about it in the summary. If your rubric line says "did it run X?", a LLM judge is guessing unless you evaluate the actual tool-call trajectory.

Takeaway: Don't grade an agent on its closing pitch. Score the raw execution trajectory to verify what commands were actually executed, validated, and scoped.

2. Design evals for asynchronous operations

When you start reading tool-call trajectories, how you extract that telemetry matters just as much as what you're reading. Extracting agent telemetry into a flattened, sequential list of events obscures concurrent tool dispatch, which is one of the critical causes of behavioral failure. Modern agent harnesses often batch multiple tool invocations into a single assistant turn using an array of calls.

In our evaluations, when an agent was asked to inspect an environment and look up documentation, the harness dispatched the skill-loading call and two documentation searches simultaneously within a single tool_calls payload. Because activating a skill is a multi-stage process, where the initial call returns a short launch stub and the subsequent turn injects the full instruction body, the instructions meant to govern the search arrived in the prompt context after the system had already executed the searches.

The system never gave the skill a dedicated turn to let its guidance influence the agent's actions. If telemetry pipelines strip out turn structures and merge calls into a flat timeline, engineers will waste days wondering why an agent disregarded unambiguous instructions that a developer embedded in a skill.

Takeaway: Preserve turn structure in telemetry extractors so you can identify when client-side parallel dispatch issues tool calls before injected guidance enters the context window. 

3. Test live runs and "dry runs" side-by-side

You need to inspect real API calls to catch harness quirks, like parallel dispatch. But if you only test your agent in one environment condition, you're flying half-blind. From day one, you need to run two conditions side-by-side: a live run and a plan-only run. In the live condition, the agent has real, sandboxed credentials and actually executes commands. This is how you see if syntax works, parameters serialize cleanly, and the agent exercises restraint before doing something destructive. 

Live runs frequently hit an unexpected permission error on step two and abort before you ever reach the behavior you’re trying to test. That's why you need the plan-only condition, where you strip credentials and tell the agent to explain what it would do without running anything. This strips out permission roadblocks and shows you the model’s pure reasoning and routing intent. Roughly half our most important findings came from the delta between the two.

For example, on one of our onboarding prompts, a live run was blocked immediately on a project list call. The plan-only run sailed right through and produced an 8,000-character plan that completely ignored organization policies, admin approvals, and governance. The live run masked a major cognitive flaw that the plan-only run exposed in seconds.

Takeaway: Run live and plan-only evaluations side by side. Live runs test actual execution and safety restraint; plan-only runs expose the model's raw reasoning and routing without getting tripped up by permission errors.

4. Use “golden sets” as durable baselines

Frontier model architectures change every few months, agent harnesses improve, and plugin manifest standards will inevitably evolve. When building the Google Cloud Developer plugin, we treated evaluations as continuous integration testing for these non-deterministic environments. That means we stress-tested the composite stack, including the harness, the live model, and the tools running together on realistic tasks.

Instead of guessing from the final text output, this approach captures the whole trajectory: what the agent thought, what commands it actually ran, and whether it solved the problem without breaking anything. Then you score that run against golden sets curated by real human experts who know what the ideal path looks like.

Takeaway: Build golden sets based on what the entire system should actually do in the wild, including your harness, model, and plugins. Models change, but those baseline runs are your safety net.

Reminder: Use evaluation suites over “one-shot” demos

A common mistake I see among engineers is what I like to call the one-shot demo. This is when someone feeds a prompt into a LLM, watches it build a complete 3D game or solves a Rubik’s cube in a single pass and calls it an eval. But in reality, this is just a vanity metric. 

To do quality work with AI, I truly believe that you need evaluation suites. Without evaluations, teams are like literally running into a dark cave blind. Engineering an enterprise-grade agent means testing the system's ability to handle multi-step interactions, manage permissions, and avoid destructive outcomes like accidentally deleting a project because you asked it to "find opportunities to save costs."

Where to go from here

Building an agent plugin or MCP server is the beginning. Shipping something you can actually trust with real cloud infrastructure requires significantly more work in evaluations to ensure it’s doing what you expect it to do. At the end of the day, the only thing that outlasts model churn is a stress-tested eval suite. Check out the Google Cloud Developer plugin documentation or explore this codelab to get started with the plugin in Antigravity.

title: From Trajectories to Differentiated Skills: Cognitive Differentiation for Self-Improving Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents tackle complex tasks through reasoning and interaction with external environments. Agent skills provide persistent, transferable capabilities that guide task planning, inform contextual decisions, support tool use, and enable executable procedures. Yet existing skill-evolution methods largely organize knowledge around skill artifacts, overlooking the functional heterogeneity within individual skills and its implications for knowledge maintenance and use. Inspired by cognitive science, we propose Cognitive Differentiation in Skill Evolution (CDSE), which evolves a unified skill through four functionally distinct yet coordinated components: Meta, Experience, Tool, and Script. CDSE extracts evidence-grounded semantic gradients from successful and failed trajectories, consolidates them by functional role, and applies component-specific updates and validation with cross-component coordination and adaptive invocation. An analysis of 500 top-ranked skill packages shows that 96.8% contain knowledge spanning at least two functional roles. Across six benchmarks, three agent models, and two execution harnesses, CDSE achieves the highest scores in all 36 settings, improving over the Base agent by 7.6 percentage points and the strongest competing method in each setting by 2.6 points on average. Ablation studies further support the importance of functional differentiation and adaptive invocation.

title: Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents
summary: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across complex tasks, they predominantly operate in isolated sessions, lacking the ability to continually learn from historical interactions or adapt to user-specific environments. Existing self-evolution paradigms often indiscriminately inject raw interaction trajectories into memory or skill modules, leading to obscured behavioral patterns and compromised update controllability. Furthermore, as foundational LLM reasoning improves, the bottleneck for agentic evolution shifts from accumulating generic knowledge to effectively managing situational experience. To address this, we propose Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive self-evolving framework that systematically distills episodic experiences to drive the comprehensive evolution of operational skills and durable memory. Theoretically grounded in an iterative agent-actor and evolver-critic co-adaptation, Darwin-Claw introduces a Hierarchical Experience Consolidation System that extracts fine-grained error attributions and generalizes them into dynamically updated prototype vectors. This structured situational experience serves as interaction patches for context-sensitive perception and explicit optimization signals for skill refinement. Practically, Darwin-Claw is a readily deployable, automated framework compatible with mainstream agent systems without requiring manual curation. Extensive experiments on WildClawBench demonstrate that Darwin-Claw yields substantial performance improvements, establishing a controllable and stable pathway for the continual, user-centric adaptation of autonomous agents in real-world ecosystems.

title: SkillBrowser: Selective Skill Exposure for Scalable Skill-Using Agents
summary: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skills to extend their capabilities in complex tasks. However, scalable skill use requires Selective Skill Exposure (SSE): providing relevant procedural content when needed while avoiding unnecessary exposure that may disrupt reasoning. Existing paradigms fall short in complementary ways. Progressive disclosure exposes metadata for a growing skill library, introducing context pollution; retrieval limits catalog exposure, but static retrieval from the initial task query may be misaligned with capability needs that emerge during reasoning and may still inject unnecessary skills. We propose SkillBrowser, a Meta-Skill-managed framework that enables an agent to identify current capability needs, formulate targeted queries, and selectively load skills on demand. Across six SRA-Bench subsets and five LLMs, SkillBrowser improves aggregate accuracy over static retrieval and LLM-based selection, including multi-step tool use, and mitigates accuracy degradation on already-solvable instances. Benefits remain model- and task-dependent, with under-invocation of useful skills and additional latency as key limitations. These results demonstrate the viability of Meta-Skill-managed SSE for scalable skill repositories.

title: codex 0.163.0
summary:
New Features

  • Open /config to search preferences across categories, change supported settings immediately, and see which changes require a restart. (#52990, #53429)
  • Send a follow-up while Codex is responding to steer it immediately. Interrupting a turn also stops active Code Mode cells and their nested tool calls. (#51812, #51835)
  • Configure a leader key in /keymap. The default is Ctrl+X, shortcut hints stay open until you choose or cancel, and voice mute moves to F9. (#52273)
  • Restart a managed background server from /daemon. Codex warns about work the restart could interrupt, then reconnects automatically. (#53173)
  • Codex can run independent read-only tools in parallel, including skill, memory, and conversation-history lookups. (#52245)
  • Daybreak is enabled by default for eligible accounts. codex exec can also select it with an OpenAI API key when the server offers access. (#53701, #53717)

Bug Fixes

  • Resuming a saved thread restores its permissions and network approvals, while respecting explicit overrides and current managed policy. (#53150, #53419, #53424)
  • The network proxy now checks permission before a DNS lookup, rejects duplicate Host headers, and prevents credential aliases from bypassing inspection hooks. (#51650, #52661, #53506)
  • Return to an existing side conversation with /side after switching threads. Answers to pending prompts also go back to the thread that asked. (#52184, #53436)
  • On Windows, Ctrl+V and Shift+Insert paste text as well as images. On WSL, repeated pastes reuse the clipboard reader, and copy attempts time out instead of hanging. (#53224, #52967, #53453)
  • Local commands finish promptly when a child keeps an output pipe open. Remote commands preserve late-arriving output so the final poll can still collect it. (#52652, #53331, #53622)
  • codex exec no longer prints the same file diff again after an unrelated command. (#53444)

Documentation

  • Updated the bundled OpenAI Docs guidance for migrations to the GPT-6 family, including model-specific reasoning, tool use, and data residency considerations. (#51768)
  • Clarified how the Linux sandbox uses bubblewrap for filesystem isolation and seccomp for syscall filtering. (#52610)

Chores

  • Codex now uses its standard shell executor and no longer bundles a patched zsh. Configurations using the retired shell flags receive a migration notice. (#52160, #52213)
  • Reduced Linux and macOS release package size by stripping symbols from packaged binaries while preserving them in the original build outputs. (#52178)

title: Chirp Pong
summary:
Tool: Chirp Pong

Another game experiment - I wanted to see if it was feasible to have a two player game on two separate phones running in static HTML where the networking code uses chirps sent via the microphone. It seems to work!

Build a two player competitive pong like game where two players use their phones close to each other and the game state is sent via audio noises which the web microphone API can interpret - but add graphical and gameplay twists to make it a lot more fun and intertwine than pong

Claude Opus 5.5 Extra in Claude Code.

title: claude-code v2.1.301
summary:
What's changed

  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS so unattended retry mode (CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG) ends a request at a usage limit that resets too far away instead of waiting
  • Added OpenTelemetry tracing guidance to the claude-api skill, including setting up trace destinations with the ant CLI
  • Added the % motion to vim mode: jump to the matching bracket, alone or with d/c/y
  • Added rows to a mod's Input: a text field of several lines in the terminal, where Enter submits and Shift+Enter or a backslash before Enter starts a new line
  • Added classifier_verdict and permission_mode to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, so auto mode classifier decisions can be told apart from permission rules
  • Added classifier_category to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, naming the built-in rule a classifier block matched, when OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1
  • Fixed quitting removing a worktree made by a WorktreeCreate hook without asking when it may hold unpushed commits
  • Fixed the fable (and best) model alias erroring on the Anthropic API when the newest Fable model is not available to your organization: Claude Code now retries once on the previous Fable model
  • Fixed a misleading "Please run /login" error when a full disk keeps the login from being refreshed; the error now names the disk and says to delete files
  • Fixed Grep and Glob reporting no matches when the search program failed unexpectedly before returning any results; they now return an error saying the search failed
  • Fixed workflow agents sometimes skipping their step, and the run still reporting success, after reading the harness note that their task text carries no user authority
  • Fixed artifact updates being refused where a PreToolUse hook covers Edit or Write; Claude now edits the file and then republishes instead of changing it in the publish call
  • Fixed skills and commands with very many or very long argument names stalling for seconds when invoked; only the first 64 names, each up to 64 characters, are now filled in
  • Fixed skills, commands and hooks using very large amounts of memory when their arguments fill many placeholders
  • Fixed stray characters such as >0q covering the folder trust prompt, and >4m before the shell prompt at exit, in terminals built on VTE older than 0.53 such as MATE Terminal on RHEL 8
  • Fixed stray GOK text appearing in the prompt at startup in some versions of iTerm2
  • Fixed switching to a model whose name contains application-inference-profile running your awsAuthRefresh command and delaying model-switch hooks when the provider is not Bedrock
  • Fixed sign-in refresh timeouts and unexpected sign-outs after a short command such as claude auth status or claude plugin list exited in the middle of a token refresh
  • Fixed a tool call cut off by a message sent mid-turn during its permission check being reported to the model as rejected by the user
  • Fixed a case where switching to a model with a smaller context window could spend usage credits on a summary by the previous model without asking first
  • Fixed conversations being compacted over and over, on a model you didn't pick, behind an LLM gateway whose responses name a different model than the one requested
  • Fixed vim mode sometimes staying in INSERT after Escape on a slow or busy machine
  • Fixed Esc discarding a typed AskUserQuestion answer in vim mode: the free-text field now supports vim NORMAL mode, and Esc cancels only from NORMAL
  • Fixed the Read tool reading binary files such as .xlsm, .parquet, .epub and .heic as text
  • Fixed a Markdown table with only a header row drawing nothing when too wide for the terminal, including in plans on the plan approval card
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill saying CMEK external-key endpoints aren't available on Claude Platform on AWS
  • Fixed skills no longer being listed to the model after using /rewind
  • Fixed the compaction row in a resumed session offering ctrl+o for history that is not loaded; it now says where the earlier messages are saved, and also shows in fullscreen
  • Fixed the "new task? /clear to save tokens" hint coming back right after you interrupt a response
  • Fixed the permission prompt for a plugin or skill hook's ask decision not showing which plugin or skill the hook comes from
  • Fixed /diff not noticing a conflicted cherry-pick or revert in reftable repositories when one of its git checks timed out or failed
  • Fixed workflow scripts asking for permission or being refused when read, edited or re-run after a Bash cd in the same session
  • Fixed dim text on the dark ANSI theme and 16-color terminals: faint inside filled boxes, not faint under selection and search highlights, and list descriptions dimmed like other secondary text
  • Fixed a mod's $.model.fork returning nothing-to-fork when called before the first response of a new Claude Code process had finished, as in claude -p runs and cloud sessions
  • Fullscreen mode: Fixed /compact and auto-compact briefly freezing the UI while the visible transcript is rebuilt
