title: How Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs
summary:
Editor's note: Generative AI startups are moving rapidly beyond static clip generation to build interactive, real-time worlds. In this technical deep dive, we explore how AI startup Visko collaborated with Google Cloud TPU engineers to deploy Orbis — its continuously streaming Live World Model—on Cloud TPUs, going from initial kickoff to production handover in just 30 days.

What makes a live video world model so challenging to serve in production? The bottleneck isn't average throughput — it's beating a relentless real-time clock. Unlike offline video generators where a user submits a prompt and waits in a queue, a live world model streams continuously. Every new chunk of video and synchronized audio must finish rendering before the viewer finishes watching the previous one, or the world freezes.

Today, we're excited to share how Visko, an AI startup pioneering interactive world models, teamed up with Google Cloud to solve this exact challenge. Working side by side, Visko and Google Cloud engineers deployed Visko's end-to-end live inference pipeline — combining video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio—onto a single Cloud TPU slice. Together, the teams brought end-to-end generation down, rendering at 1.07x playback speed.

Here is an inside look at how we engineered the pipeline to hit that milestone in a single month, the architectural optimizations that moved the needle, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI on Google Cloud.

Redefining interactive media with Live World Models

While most generative video platforms focus on rendering fixed, pre-baked clips, Visko is building what it calls Live Models: video world models that generate continuously and respond on the fly.

Visko's flagship model, Orbis, streams live video starting from a single text or image prompt. As the stream plays, viewers can enter new steering prompts in real time, dynamically evolving the scene without restarting or breaking continuity. For instance, in one test session, the livestream opens on a cat napping beside a crackling fireplace; when the viewer steers the scene to introduce a bowl of food, the bowl materializes seamlessly, and the cat stretches, stands up, and meows.

Since launching its public demo on September 1, 2026, Orbis has unlocked new possibilities across interactive entertainment, live commerce, AI companions, immersive education, and robotics simulation. To scale these interactive sessions reliably, Visko partnered with Google Cloud TPU engineers in August 2026 to port the Orbis live pipeline to Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). Within 30 days, the full multimodal pipeline was running in real time on TPUs.

Visko’s ambition is to power a new generation of interactive worlds that people can step into and shape in real time. Streaming continuous video and audio under a strict clock is a fundamentally different system challenge than offline clip generation. Working side by side with Google Cloud's TPU engineers, we brought the full Orbis pipeline to TPUs in just 30 days — giving us the low-latency compute and memory bandwidth required to bring Live Models to creators and developers at scale.

"Visko is bringing an exciting new class of real-time, steerable workloads to the Cloud TPU ecosystem. By co-engineering their live multimodal pipeline on a singleTPU slice using JAX, torchax, and custom Pallas kernels, we proved how quickly a lean startup team can go from PyTorch prototype to render at 1.07x playback speed on Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer."
– Dave Elliott, Head of Developer Advocacy for AI, Google Cloud 

Live video is a hard-deadline problem

When you serve an offline clip generator, latency is forgiving — the user waits once while the backend processes frames. A live world model has no waiting room.

Every single chunk must be denoised, decoded from latents, upscaled to 1664x936 (at 18 fps), and paired with generated audio faster than realtime playback speed, for as long as the session runs.

Two structural constraints make live world models far more demanding than standard batch inference:

  • Batch size of one: Each live stream represents an individual viewer's interactive session. You cannot mask latency by grouping dozens of concurrent requests into a massive batch — the standard playbook for keeping AI accelerators saturated.

  • Strict sequential dependency: Every chunk depends directly on the one before it. Because the video model maintains a rolling memory of recent video latents so that chunk N+1 smoothly continues the action from chunk N, you cannot pre-render chunks out of order or parallelize across future timestamps.

For startup infrastructure engineers coming from LLM serving, it helps to think of live world modeling not as a tokens-per-second throughput benchmark, but as an unforgiving per-step latency SLO.

Architecting the multimodal pipeline on a single TPU slice

To keep infrastructure lean and cost-effective as Visko scales, the team designed the live pipeline to chain three distinct generative models on a single Cloud TPU slice running in BF16 precision.

When a viewer submits an initial prompt or a live steering update, all three generative models — the core video diffusion model, the super-resolution upscaler, and the audio generator — share the same chips, taking turns on the hardware for each chunk.

To combine rapid startup iteration with bare-metal accelerator speed, the software stack is built on three open-source pillars:

  • JAX: Google's high-performance Python array library for accelerators, compiled into optimized machine code by the XLA compiler.

  • torchax: An interoperability layer that runs PyTorch models directly on Cloud TPUs via JAX, enabling startup teams to bring existing PyTorch components over without an upfront, ground-up rewrite.

  • Pallas: The custom kernel programming language for TPUs in JAX.

Real-time performance breakdown: Hitting the clock 

By profiling and optimizing each stage on a single slice in BF16, the engineering team achieved a total per-chunk latency of under the target while — maintaining roughly 7% headroom to absorb variance during live streaming:

Because video denoising accounts for nearly two-thirds of the total compute budget, that stage became the primary focus of our kernel and parallelism optimizations.

Inside the stack: Three optimizations that unlocked real-time streaming

1. Ulysses context parallelism across all TPU chips

A video chunk expands into a massive sequence of spatiotemporal tokens inside the video transformer. To distribute that workload across the TPU chips at batch size 1, the team implemented Ulysses context parallelism.

Instead of splitting model weights, Ulysses splits the token sequence across chips. Immediately before the attention layer, a high-speed all-to-all interconnect exchange regroups the tensors so that each chip holds the entire video sequence, but only for one-quarter of the attention heads. After each chip computes attention over the full sequence for its assigned heads, a second all-to-all exchange restores the sequence-split layout for the feed-forward layers.

2. Custom Pallas splash attention from MaxDiffusion

To accelerate the attention computation itself, the team integrated a custom Pallas splash attention kernel from MaxDiffusion, Google Cloud's open-source reference library for diffusion models on Cloud TPU.

Splash attention brings FlashAttention-style tiling to TPU architecture: rather than materializing the full quadratic attention matrix in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), it computes attention in compact tiles that remain inside ultra-fast on-chip VMEM. Startup teams can drop the exact kernel used in this port straight into their own pipelines via custom_splash_attention.py.

3. A 5.8x audio speedup by moving from torchax to pure JAX

We first brought all three Orbis models onto Cloud TPU with torchax, which runs PyTorch code on TPU through JAX and XLA without a rewrite. For the video and upscaling models, torchax paired with Pallas attention kernels met our latency target directly, and both stay in torchax in the final pipeline.

Only the audio model needed a rewrite. Moving the audio stage from torchax to native JAX made it 5.8x faster and brought the full pipeline under the playback deadline.

Field notes for AI builders: Cloud TPU lessons

Takeaways from tuning live multimodal inference on Cloud TPU:

  • Ulysses context parallelism for single stream video: At batch size 1, splitting the token sequence across chips with all-to-all interconnect exchanges was faster than both tensor parallelism and ring attention.
  • Native BF16 for continuous streams: FP8 quantization cuts memory bandwidth pressure, but small quantization errors build up across chunks in a continuous stream. Native BF16 kept visual quality intact within the latency budget.
  • Selective JAX ports: torchax kept the video and upscaling models in PyTorch, so the team only rewrote the audio bottleneck in native JAX.
  • XLA compilation caching: The first boot spends a few minutes compiling XLA graphs. Caching compiled artifacts brings worker restarts under a minute.

Building real-time generative models on Cloud TPU? Start here

If your startup is pushing the boundaries of live video, world models, or ultra-low-latency multimodal inference, you can build with the same toolkit that powered Visko's port:

  • Accelerate diffusion attention out of the box: Grab the open-source splash attention kernel used in this collaboration from MaxDiffusion, and explore the Pallas documentation to write custom TPU kernels.

  • Migrate PyTorch fast, then optimize selectively: Bring your existing PyTorch models onto TPU quickly with torchax, pinpoint bottlenecks with the Cloud TPU Profiler, and port latency-critical stages to native JAX.

  • Spin up TPUs on demand: Use TPU Flex-start VMs to provision TPU capacity for short development and benchmarking runs without a long-term reservation.

  • Scale with Google for Startups: Early-stage AI startups looking for cloud credits, technical mentorship, and access to Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer stack can apply to the Google for Startups Cloud Program.

Special thanks to the Visko.ai team for the close technical partnership, and to the Google Cloud TPU engineers who lead the project including: Yixin Shi, James Huang, and Elisa Tsai.

title: What the Gemini agent means for startups
summary:
Small teams, short runway, and constant pressure to ship faster — it’s the reality we see every day among the founders we work with at Google for Startups. When you are building a company from the ground up, every hour spent on operational overhead or infrastructure plumbing is an hour taken away from your core product.

Last week at Gemini at Work 2026, we introduced the Gemini agent: a single, universal agent designed to work both as your personal assistant and as a dedicated member of your team. And this week, we made our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, widely available — trained to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks.

Here is a look at how the Gemini agent works, five practical takeaways for founders, and how startups are already using it to punch above their weight.

What is the Gemini agent?

Instead of prompting separate chatbots for writing, coding, and data analysis, the Gemini agent is a single agent that takes high-level objectives and returns finished work. Three principles define it:

  • Unified: A single agent can now handle knowledge work, data analysis, creative asset generation, and writing and running code. For complex jobs, it dynamically spins up temporary, job-specific sub-agents and coordinates their work in parallel or in sequence.

  • Omnipresent access: It works across the surfaces you use every day — on the web, command line, desktop, and mobile, as well as natively inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Chat, and Calendar.

  • Persistent: It runs in the cloud with continuous memory across four dimensions (session, semantic, procedural, and episodic). It onboards itself like a new hire — learning your team, tools, and business context so you don't have to re-explain your startup with every prompt, and keeping multi-day tasks moving even after you close your laptop.

For founders wearing five hats at once, Gemini works like a digital chief of staff that's already briefed on your calendar, projects and documents. Ask it to research market trends, build a financial model in Sheets and turn both into a pitch deck, without repeating what the project or goals are at each step. It also works ahead of you. When an investor emails asking for your latest product update as a deck, Gemini spots the request and offers to handle it; one click and it comes back with completed work, ready for sharing or review.

Five takeaways for startups

1. Coworker agents and skills help you scale your output

Beyond personal assistance, you can create persistent coworker agents that work with your entire team. Each agent comes with its own Workspace account, email address, Drive storage, and directory presence. You can define a specific role — such as a launch coordinator, QA triager, or financial analyst — and your teammates can add agents to a Chat space or @mention it in a Google Doc comment to delegate work.

You can also equip agents with reusable skills — or let Gemini write skills for itself as it learns your processes. For example, with operational reporting skills connected to BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog, anyone on your team can ask a plain-language question to build and save a live report. Once saved, those reports run on demand without incurring additional token costs. Gemini also offers pre-built specializations, starting with legal and financial services.

  • What it means for startups: Coworker agents can immediately increase the capacity of your teams, and skills can standardize repeatable processes like investor and operational reporting without burning tokens on every run.

2. Open and third-party model choice

Gemini is the agent, and the model underneath is your choice. As startup architectures mature, sending every task to a single frontier model quickly eats into gross margins. With the Gemini agent, you can dynamically route workloads across Gemini models, third-party models like Anthropic’s Claude, and lightweight open models like Gemma.

  • What it means for startups: You get flexibility without lock-in. You can optimize your cost per task — using compact models for high-volume, deterministic jobs and frontier models for complex reasoning — and swap models as your product evolves without rebuilding your workflows.

3. Connected to your services and tools 

An agent is only as useful as the systems it can reach. In addition to Google Workspace, the Gemini agent connects directly to your engineering, data, and business stack, including partner solutions:

  • Development and collaboration: Git, Slack, Jira and more 

  • Data and local files: BigQuery, Postgres, Snowflake, Databricks, and more alongside files on your desktop

  • Custom tools via MCP: Any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside your network so your engineers can build and share internal tools.

What it means for startups: Instead of spending engineering cycles maintaining custom connectors, your team can plug the agent straight into your existing codebase, databases, and MCP tools so it can act on live data wherever it lives.

4. Built-in security and governance

For B2B startups, the enterprise security audit is often where deals stall. Under the hood, every agent is assigned a cryptographic Agent Identity for clear audit trails, runs inside an isolated sandbox, and protected with built-in prompt injection defenses. External traffic is routed through Agent Gateway, allowing you to enforce governance policies. And managing coworker agents is as straightforward as managing users today, since they all have a Workspace account.

  • What it means for startups: When an enterprise buyer’s CISO asks how your AI workflows handle data privacy, prompt injection, and access control, you have an enterprise-grade architecture ready — helping you clear procurement hurdles.

5. Protect your runway with real-time cost controls

Autonomous agents that run sub-agents for hours or days can quickly run up a bill if a loop goes unchecked. You can now set hard, real-time spend caps directly in the Cloud Billing Console; if a cap is reached, the project's agent automatically pauses so a bug never turns into a billing surprise. Underneath, Gemini runs on Google’s specialized AI infrastructure, including our inference-optimized TPU 8i, which delivers 80% better performance-per-dollar than the prior generation.

  • What it means for startups: You and your developers can experiment with long-running, parallel agentic loops with a built-in financial safety net that protects your cash reserves and builds confidence with your backers.

Founders already building

Startups and AI-native innovators are already putting Gemini to work. Immersive storytelling platform Whenere used Dreamlands, an agentic 3D worldbuilding platform built on Gemini platform, to bring Pride and Prejudice to Fortnite — with Gemini generating textures for each new object in about 7 seconds for under 10 cents; one artist created nearly 250 custom assets in a single day and completed a historically accurate estate in under a week. They join application-building platform Lovable and fellow startups and innovators including  OpenEvidence, Recursion, and Replit and more.

Build with Google for Startups

The agentic era gives lean teams the leverage to punch far above their weight — whether you’re deploying coworker agents to cover internal operations or building agentic workflows directly into your product.

While these new Gemini agent capabilities are not publicly available yet, startups can contact our sales team to learn more and discuss how to get ready. In the meantime, you can explore the Google for Startups program to access credits, hands-on technical guidance, mentorship, global founder community programs and more.

title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
summary:
Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO

The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from "people with knowledge of the matter".

Key things I learned from the article:

  • Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn"
  • Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn
  • Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn
  • In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power"
  • Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11%

This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine):

The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones.

When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending.

Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter!

Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" (previously) in these communications to their investors.

title: Qwen-Audio-Jev: A Unified Interface for Audio Decisions
summary: Large audio language models (LALMs) have made substantial progress in audio understanding. However, in high-throughput applications requiring frequent selection, judgment, and scoring, autoregressive text generation introduces additional computational overhead and response latency. To address this limitation, we introduce Qwen-Audio-Jev by augmenting Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next with a dedicated Jev decision head. The model unifies selection, binary judgment, and scoring through three decision primitives: CHOICE, NOUL, and SCORE. Given audio, a natural-language question, and an explicit answer specification, it directly produces a task-conditioned probability distribution or a numerical score through typed decision readouts. Evaluation across 18 labeled configurations covers all three primitives: for CHOICE, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves accuracies of 78.70% on MMAU-mini and 84.06% on MMSU; for NOUL, it achieves an equal error rate of 6.50% on the VoxCeleb1-O speaker verification benchmark; and for SCORE, the model achieves a normalized mean absolute error of 0.1062 on NISQA overall quality assessment, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.8210 and 0.8074, respectively. Compared with the original Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves an approximately 20x inference speedup. It demonstrates its potential for efficient, high-throughput audio decision-making in applications such as large-scale audio screening, speaker verification, and automated quality assessment.

title: LaTeX renderer
summary:
Tool: LaTeX renderer

Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office, which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner).

Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link.

It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works:

Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used:

I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too.

Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks:

Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project

I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well:

We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool

Here's an example link. The tool uses Pako 2.1.0, MathJax 4.1.3, faster-latex 0.3.1, and DOMPurify 3.4.16.

Tool: Tree Appreciator

Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with:

Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.

Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk, I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play.

title: claude-code v2.1.300
summary:
What's changed

  • Added virtualText to a mod's prompt decorations: text drawn in the prompt box that never enters the draft or the submitted prompt
  • Added cache_creation_5m_tokens and cache_creation_1h_tokens to the OpenTelemetry api_request event, splitting cache writes by lifetime
  • Added $.ui.view({ agentId }) for mods: shows an agent's transcript in the main view when you ask, and $.ui.view({}) goes back
  • Added a dir prop on a mod's Text for right-to-left text: on Windows and in VS Code's terminal its rows read in that direction and sit flush right
  • Added /advisor on Claude Platform on AWS; no advisor runs until you pick one with /advisor, advisorModel or --advisor, and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL=1 turns it off
  • Added OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic-convention attributes to trace spans, such as gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.conversation.id, gen_ai.tool.name and error.type
  • Added support for rewriting a workflow agent's prompt and model in the agent.spawn mod hook, which could only refuse workflow agents before
  • Added the prompt.change mod hook, raised when the prompt box's text changes without a typed edit: a recalled history entry, a clear, an undo, or a plugin's fill
  • Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude that an organization policy blocked a host when the session's own network settings did
  • Fixed /autocompact warning about high token usage when you choose a smaller auto-compact window
  • Fixed SessionEnd hooks sometimes not running when you exit while a background command is still running
  • Fixed claude --help naming a removed tool in its description of --restricted
  • Fixed claude agents not refreshing any pull request's status when the data for one of them came back incomplete
  • Fixed Claude being told a background agent was lost, not resumable, after a cloud session's container was replaced, when the agent had already been resumed once
  • Fixed subagents you had typed messages to disappearing from /tasks shortly after finishing, leaving no way back to the conversation
  • Fixed a completed parent agent dropping off the breadcrumb (its child shown re-rooted at top level) while you were viewing the child
  • Fixed the agents view taking a typed word such as "up", "down" or "escape" for that key when input arrived in a burst, which could move the peek mid-reply or clear a draft
  • Fixed automatic tool search (ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto) turning off part-way through a conversation, for example while MCP servers reconnect after a resume
  • Fixed a login refused by forceLoginOrgUUID leaving the refused organization's token stored, or live after /login
  • Fixed the diff view in Claude Desktop and Remote Control sessions not noticing a conflicted cherry-pick or revert in reftable repositories
  • Fixed the Artifact tool's verbose and ctrl+o line reading Artifact("(unprintable path)") while a call's input arrives; its row now shows "Waiting…" and "Running…" as Bash's does
  • Fixed the first transcript entry written after resuming a session being lost when a crash had cut the transcript's last line short
  • Fixed /branch dropping messages, and claude purge skipping subfolder projects, when they contain a Unicode line or paragraph separator (U+2028, U+2029)
  • Fixed plugin WorktreeCreate and WorktreeRemove hooks not running when Claude Code starts with --worktree (not yet with --tmux)
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry tool_result events missing git_commit_id after git commit -q in repositories using reftable ref storage
  • Fixed a prompt that a mod's prompt.submit hook rewrote or dropped still being recorded as typed in the OpenTelemetry user_prompt event and interaction span, and in session title requests
  • Fixed a note meant for Claude about mod hot-reloading appearing in the transcript as if you had typed it
  • Fixed agent hooks ignoring their model: aliases like haiku now resolve, a subagent's model no longer overrides it, and an unavailable model falls back to the caller's instead of allowing the action
  • Fixed --worktree sessions sometimes starting from the wrong commit when a tag or branch was named like a commit ID, and their starting git status naming a branch other than the new worktree's
  • Fixed the branch showing as ".invalid" and --worktree failing to reopen a worktree in repositories using git's reftable ref storage
  • Fixed Claude naming files in the session scratchpad by a bare filename or relative path instead of their full path
  • Fixed claude remote-control servers giving up on renewing their connection after a brief sign-in error, such as a locked keychain; they now retry, and warn when you need to run claude /login
  • Fixed --worktree failing in a worktree of a bare repository when origin's default branch can't be fetched; the fallback base is now the current checkout's HEAD, not the main repository's
  • Fixed starting Claude Code in a VS Code, Cursor or Devin Desktop integrated terminal launching the editor's command-line tool twice to check for the extension; it now launches it once
  • Fixed a mod's prompt.edit hook not being raised for a newline entered with the chat:newline keybinding (Ctrl+J, or a rebound Enter)
  • Fixed a conversation failing on every turn with a 400 error when the API rejected an MCP tool's input schema; Claude Code now sends that tool without parameters for the rest of the conversation
  • Fixed resuming a headless or Agent SDK session losing the recent messages a compaction had kept, when the compaction followed a reply cut at the output token limit (compactions from this version on)
  • Fixed Claude not being told about an MCP server's tools and instructions until its next tool call, when the server finished connecting after a compaction
  • Fixed Remote Control sessions being marked stopped while still running, on a computer serving several sessions at once
  • Fixed resuming a headless or Agent SDK session losing its compaction summary or bringing back pre-compaction history, when the compaction followed a retried or unfinished reply in the same turn
  • Fixed Claude polling a background command's output file or sleeping while it runs
  • Fixed feature flags and staged rollouts staying stale behind a TLS-inspecting proxy whose certificate is trusted only through the OS certificate store
  • Fixed claude daemon stop --any printing "stopped" while a stuck background service kept running: it now waits, force-kills the service, and says so with exit 1 if it is still there
  • Fixed claude daemon stop exiting with no output, and leaving sessions listed as running, when telemetry is turned off
  • Fixed Write, Edit and NotebookEdit in Cowork cloud sessions reporting success for a path on your own computer, where the file never arrived
  • Fixed Claude searching for deferred tools already loaded earlier in the conversation when a session resumes a history that never listed them
  • Fixed secondary (dim) text looking the same as normal text under the dark ANSI theme and on 16-color terminals
  • Fixed cloud sessions hanging 5 minutes per turn when the organization's policy can't be read; the turn now ends promptly and says why
  • Fixed a cloud session sometimes running an already answered message a second time after the session restarted during a long reply
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed the runner and orchestrator freezing (no polls, /healthz or SIGTERM shutdown) while nobody reads their output; logs keep the latest 256 KiB and count drops (not on Windows)
  • Improved WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions to tell Claude that a page failed moments ago instead of fetching it again
  • Improved mod sharing in the built-in plugin-authoring skill: Claude scans a mod's files for keys before opening them, and asks before scanning a folder outside the project
  • Improved the note Claude 3 models get about an @-mentioned PDF, so they less often answer without reading it
  • Improved artifact updates: Claude now applies a small change and republishes the artifact in one call, and makes larger edits and republishes within a single response
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_PROVIDER_MANAGED_BY_HOST sessions to ignore CA-bundle, tool-proxy, git TLS and git config variables like SSL_CERT_FILE in settings; under Claude Desktop, only in project settings
  • Changed exit to force-kill background commands still running 1.5 seconds after being asked to stop; in fullscreen mode they could previously be left running
  • Changed Claude Desktop's Code tab to apply managed settings when forceLoginGatewayUrl names an Anthropic-operated gateway that serves the session's hostname; that gateway must be reachable at start
  • Changed claude gateway to stop at start, naming the key, on a desktop: policy key that Claude Desktop cannot use from a gateway, where it earlier started with a warning
  • Changed large requests to api.anthropic.com to use gzip compression even when telemetry is disabled; set CLAUDE_CODE_GZIP_REQUEST_BODIES=0 to turn it off
  • Changed the claude-api skill to leave Managed Agents sessions in place unless you ask to archive or delete them
  • Changed background sessions to resume a carried workflow through the Workflow tool's approval instead of running it from the handoff file
  • Changed local session transcripts to also record each API request's system prompt, tools and parameters, so a transcript you choose to share can reproduce a request exactly
  • Changed the /sandbox mode options to read "Sandbox commands" instead of "Sandbox BashTool"
  • Changed PermissionRequest hooks in Cowork cloud sessions: a setMode update in a hook's allow is now ignored; the rest of the approval still applies
  • Changed hooks: updatedInput from PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks is now validated like Claude's own input: unknown keys are dropped, and input the tool rejects denies the call
  • Removed the --sandbox and --no-sandbox flags from claude remote-control, which had no effect; passing either now exits with an error. Set sandbox.enabled in settings to sandbox sessions
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.attachSelection setting to stop text selected in the editor from being added to your messages
  • [VSCode] Fixed fast mode staying on after usage credits ran out, which made each request be refused and re-sent; it now turns off until you turn it back on, with an error notice
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Thinking toggle switching to Off on models that always think; the toggle is no longer shown for those models
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Edit prompt" on a flagged message opening the file or command menu over the restored prompt; Enter now sends it as written
  • [VSCode] Fixed Shift+dragging a file onto the prompt on Windows inserting an unreadable /c:/… path instead of a mention relative to the working directory
  • [VSCode] Fixed changes to VS Code's chat font size settings needing a window reload or being undone by a theme change; diffs and the plan preview now follow them too
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Resume session" and tabs restored after a reload opening an empty new conversation instead of one that had moved into a git worktree
  • [VSCode] Fixed ↑ then Enter on a recalled slash command running it without its arguments; the command and file menus no longer open over a recalled prompt until you edit it
  • [VSCode] Fixed Shift+dragging a file from the Explorer or an editor tab onto the prompt inserting nothing in WSL, SSH and Dev Container windows
  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+Alt+F toggling Focus view instead of opening Find in the Explorer, other tree views, or the Debug Console on Windows and Linux
  • [VSCode] Fixed the check for sessions open in other windows or terminals creating extra processes on macOS: it now starts /bin/ps directly instead of searching PATH for ps on every check
  • [VSCode] Windows: Fixed a conversation showing "still open somewhere else" after a crash or power loss, when Windows had since restarted and given the old process ID to another program
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed "Allow for this task" missing from Cowork's approval prompts for connector tools where an organization turns off "Always allow" (regression in 2.1.292)
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed most commands in the / menu losing their descriptions in cloud sessions once you sent a second message
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the diff view in Remote Control sessions on claude.ai and the desktop app showing deleted and renamed files as modified; requires Claude Code v2.1.296 or later on your machine
  • [Claude Tag] Added support for Slack Connect channels: an Owner or Claude Tag admin can let Claude in Slack answer in channels shared with another organization; it's off by default
  • [Claude Tag] Added a private Allow once / Deny card in Slack threads for connector actions that need your approval, so Claude asks instead of refusing; others only see that it's waiting on you
  • [Claude Tag] Added support for Slack voice clips in Claude in Slack: Claude reads Slack's transcript of a clip when Slack has one
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not answering another app that tags it in a thread under a message Claude itself posted to the channel
  • [Claude Tag] Changed access bundles an admin attached to a Slack channel to keep applying once the channel becomes a Slack Connect channel, with no need to remove and re-attach them
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review ignoring @claude review comments from people with write access whose GitHub organization membership is private; their comments now start a review
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review's "paused for this repository" comment sending admins to Code Review settings; it now says who can fix it and links the Git providers page

title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
summary:
AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.

Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly).

I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development:

Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...]

This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[

With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.

Via Hacker News

title: Predictable AI spend in BigQuery: Introducing cost management for generative AI functions
summary:
The generative AI functions in BigQuery (AI.GENERATE, AI.IF, AI.CLASSIFY, AI.SCORE, and more) bring large language models (LLMs) directly into your SQL, so a single query can classify millions of support tickets or score each product review for sentiment. However, because these functions are billed by the token, scaling them across massive datasets highlights the importance of managing your budget proactively. 

We recently announced the general availability (GA) of token-based cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions: daily quotas that let administrators set self-serve guardrails on AI token consumption, so teams can innovate while staying within your budget. In this blog, we provide an overview of cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions, walk through a few practical examples, and share resources to help you get started. Let’s jump in.  

Quotas for managing costs

Four daily quotas, managed through the Google Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM) quota system, provide controls at the project level and the per-user level. Per-user limits apply to each user within a project, not across your organization.

Key details:

  • The quotas are global. Usage is summed across all regions, so costs can't pile up unnoticed in a region you weren't watching.

  • Output quotas include "thinking" tokens. Reasoning tokens count toward your output quota, just as they count toward your Gemini platform bill.

Which functions are covered?

The quotas apply to these BigQuery functions that perform LLM-backed generation:

  • AI.GENERATE

  • AI.GENERATE_TABLE

  • AI.GENERATE_TEXT (and its alias ML.GENERATE_TEXT)

  • AI.CLASSIFY

  • AI.IF

  • AI.SCORE

  • AI.AGG

What's not covered: Embedding functions such as AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING (also available as ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING) and AI.EMBED are not subject to these quotas, because they run on different, substantially cheaper models.

Managing your quotas

Administrators can view and adjust the quotas directly in the Google Cloud console as workloads change, with no support case required.

  1. Navigate to IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

  2. Filter by service and select BigQuery API.

  3. Sort by the Name column to bring the four AI quotas to the top.

4. Find the quota, for example AI input tokens per day.

5. Open the three-dot menu and choose Edit quota.

From there:

  • To tighten cost control, lower a quota. This takes effect immediately with no approval needed.

  • To support higher usage, request an increase from the same page. Many requests are auto-approved; larger increases may go through a quick review.

You'll need the right permissions. You need one of: Owner, Editor, Quota Administrator (roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin), or Service Usage Admin (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin).

Prefer automation? You can also manage these quotas programmatically through the Cloud Quotas API, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform to apply consistent guardrails across projects.

Monitoring usage

Beyond setting limits, the Quotas & System Limits page displays your historical token consumption so you can quickly detect spikes and right-size your budgets. Use these trends to see how new generative AI workloads and data pipelines affect your overall token usage.

For a step-by-step walkthrough, see the BigQuery documentation on controlling costs with token quotas.

Token quotas vs. billing spend caps

Token quotas aren't the only cost guardrail in Google Cloud.

  • Token quotas (this feature) are preventive and AI-specific. BigQuery tracks token usage during query execution and stops work close to the limit, with separate limits per project and per user.

  • Cloud Billing spend caps operate on dollars at the project and service level and can automatically block usage when a threshold is reached. They're a broad, financial backstop rather than a precise usage control, and because enforcement is not instant, some overages are incurred.

Use token quotas as your first line of defense for AI spend, and a spend cap as a project-wide safety net.

How enforcement works

Quotas are enforced by stopping work rather than letting a query run past your limit. A query is rejected up front with a QuotaExceeded error only if a quota it needs is already exhausted. Otherwise, it starts, and if a quota runs out mid-query, BigQuery stops sending new LLM calls:

  • Functions that support max_error_ratio (such as AI.IF) return partial results if unprocessed rows stay within the ratio, and otherwise fail.

  • General-purpose functions (such as AI.GENERATE) still succeed. Skipped rows have no generated value, and their status field contains the quota-exceeded error.

For details, see quota enforcement behavior in the documentation.

Sizing your input data: AI.COUNT_TOKENS

To choose quota values, it helps to know how much text your workloads send to a model. The AI.COUNT_TOKENS function helps with this.

AI.COUNT_TOKENS returns the number of tokens a model's tokenizer produces for a text string, without making a billable generation call. Run it over a column to measure your input data:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Count the input text tokens for each product review\r\nSELECT\r\n SUM(\r\n AI.COUNT_TOKENS(\r\n CONCAT('Classify the sentiment of this review as positive, negative, or neutral: ', review_text),\r\n\r\n endpoint => 'gemini-3.1-flash-lite').result) AS total_input_tokens\r\nFROM\r\n `my_project.my_dataset.product_reviews`;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fb5228c46d0>)])]>

The count is a lower bound on input tokens. It doesn't include output or thinking tokens, the instructions each AI function adds around your input, or non-text inputs such as images. Use it to:

  • Gauge the input side of a workload before you launch it.

  • Right-size your quotas together with a small sample run that measures actual input and output usage.

  • Translate tokens into dollars using the published Gemini platform pricing for your model.

From tokens to budget: a worked example

Suppose you want to keep a project's daily AI spend around $100 with the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite model. As of today's published pricing (BigQuery processes in batch which provides a 50% discount):

  • Input tokens: $0.125 per 1 million tokens

  • Output tokens (response + reasoning): $0.75 per 1 million tokens

If a small sample run shows an average 100:1 input-to-output token ratio, you can solve for a daily budget:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Cost: 0.125 × I + 0.75 × O = 100 (I, O in millions of tokens)\r\nRatio: I = 100 × O'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fb523106b90>)])]>

Solving gives about 754 million input tokens and 7.54 million output tokens per day. Set AI input tokens per day and AI output tokens per day to these values to hold the project near $100/day. If a project uses models with different prices, budget per model or blend the rates.

Best practices for managing AI cost

  • Start with per-user quotas. They stop one user or runaway experiment from draining the project's budget.

  • Measure before you scale. Use AI.COUNT_TOKENS to size your input, then check a small sample run in the usage chart before setting limits.

  • Mind the output side. Output tokens cost more. Where a function accepts max_output_tokens, set it to bound generation length.

  • Monitor and iterate. Adjust limits as real usage and budgets change.

Get started

Token-based cost management is available now. To begin:

  1. Open IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits in the Google Cloud Console and filter by BigQuery API.

  2. Review the four AI-related token quotas and set limits that match your budget.

  3. Use AI.COUNT_TOKENS to size your input data.

For the full details, see the documentation on controlling generative AI costs.

With token-based guardrails in place, your teams can use generative AI in BigQuery with the cost predictability your organization needs.

title: Qwen-MT-Lumen at WMT2026: Instruction-Specialized Translation via Quality-Aware Training and On-Policy Distillation
summary: We present Lumen, The open-source model is available at, our submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation Shared Task. We focus on instruction-specialized translation, where systems must produce accurate translations while satisfying fine-grained requirements on style, terminology, and structured output. Lumen follows a four-stage pipeline. First, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning jointly strengthen multilingual translation competence and the ability to follow translation-specific instructions, such as terminology, style, and format constraints. Second, we extend the originally offline M^{2}PO preference-optimization framework into an online preference-optimization stage: the current policy samples candidate translations, an LLM judge assigns continuous direct-assessment scores, and the resulting multi-pair preferences are used to update the model. Third, on-policy distillation transfers stronger translation-instruction-following behavior from a larger teacher model to the Qwen3-14B student, improving translation-instruction adherence while retaining a 14B primary translation backbone. Finally, structure-aware inference and postprocessing preserve required formats, while selective repair addresses clear structural or decoding failures before submission. We participate in 23 translation directions. Under an absolute 1--5 LLM-judge rubric that evaluates translation-instruction following and translation quality separately, Lumen reaches an overall mean score of 4.60. Despite using a 14B translation backbone, it achieves performance comparable to leading proprietary systems in both translation quality and translation-instruction following.

title: claude-code v2.1.299
summary:
What's changed

  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS environment variable: Claude gets the paths of @ file mentions to read with its file tools, not the files' contents
  • Added idle compaction in the terminal: a 200K+ token conversation left idle for about 54 minutes is compacted before its one-hour prompt cache expires, so your next message doesn't reprocess it all
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_COMPACT_MIN_TOKENS to change idle compaction's 200K-token minimum; "idleCompaction": false in settings.json turns it off. Both need v2.1.290 or later
  • Added $.prompt.media so a prompt.submit hook of a mod installed by managed settings can read the bytes of an image or document attached to the prompt
  • Added $.session.identity() for mods installed by managed settings: how the session is signed in, and its organization and email when managed forceLoginOrgUUID lists that organization
  • Added size, weight, mono and tabular to a mod's Text and named spacing steps (xs to xl) to its Box; bold is deprecated in favor of weight
  • Added --shutdown-drain-sec to claude self-hosted-runner orchestrator: on SIGTERM it stops polling and gives the poll in flight and running spawn hooks up to that many seconds to finish
  • Added the skill's frontmatter, source, plugin name and file path to what a mod's skill.prompt hook receives
  • Added /effort and /fast in agent view to set what new sessions start with; a bare /model, /effort or /fast there now opens a picker
  • Added a "safe mode" line to the agents view peek panel for background sessions started with --safe-mode
  • Added a one-time note when plan mode won't ask before most edits or commands because bypass permissions is available
  • Added --disallow-tools and a disallowed_tools case field to claude plugin eval to keep specific built-in tools, such as Agent, out of eval runs
  • Added support for turning off the attribution block in Claude Desktop's Code tab: set CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0 in the env of a Claude apps gateway's code policy
  • Added a field to the attribution block in Claude Code sessions behind a Claude apps gateway; remove the block with CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0
  • Added a queue door to the session.append mod hook, so a mod can make the transcript's queue records differ from the prompt as sent
  • Added a note in /plugin and claude plugin validate naming a mod's hooks that are skipped where an organization manages Claude Code
  • Added /usage warnings for max effort, workflows, always-on context and large tool results
  • Fixed the error for a denied cloud session, which could point to the wrong organization when a key from apiKeyHelper was in use
  • Fixed sessions on a gateway-specific model name behind a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL ending with "Prompt is too long · automatic compaction failed" near 200K tokens instead of sending the request
  • Fixed a mod that submits a prompt at the end of every turn keeping a headless run going past --max-turns, --max-budget-usd, an interrupt, or the end of the host's conversation
  • Fixed cloud sessions sometimes showing the model's follow-up text after a tool group's one-line label
  • Fixed the Write and Edit tools creating a mod in a session's mods folder without asking in accept-edits mode when the config directory's path has no .claude in it
  • Fixed installed mods that kept running in an open session after being turned off remotely; they now unload between turns
  • Fixed Edit and Retry in Cowork and claude.ai cloud sessions failing on a message stopped while its UserPromptSubmit or mod prompt.submit hooks were still running (regression in 2.1.296)

  • Fixed the claude.ai view of a Remote Control or cloud session freezing when a large batch of events could not finish uploading over a slow connection
  • Fixed a sandboxed shell command being able to write into a --plugin-dir folder, whose code Claude Code reloads and runs outside the sandbox
  • Fixed memory growth under heavy debug logging (--debug, --debug-file), and a hang on exit when the debug log is on a disk or network mount that stops accepting writes

  • Fixed scheduled tasks and loops firing again after every turn, or firing early, during the repeated hour when daylight saving time ends

  • Fixed MCP tool calls in headless and SDK sessions sometimes failing or running twice when a background reconnect closed the connection they were running on
  • Fixed /btw side questions in non-interactive sessions not being cancelled when the session ends, and running a second time when the same request arrived again mid-run
  • Fixed sandboxed commands on macOS being able to read or write a denied path by its real location when the denied path passes through a symlink
  • Fixed sandbox denyRead and allowRead globs with braces, parentheses or backslashes in a folder's name being read differently by Claude Code's settings checks than by the sandbox
  • Fixed sandbox glob allowRead and allowWrite entries not being re-checked when the directory they start from is replaced by a symlink
  • Fixed worktree-isolated sessions accepting some awk programs the isolation guard should refuse
  • Fixed claude mcp add <name> -- <command> --background being started as a background session
  • Fixed a prompt or reply of --bg or --background to a background session being taken for the flag, which could start new sessions over and over instead of delivering it
  • Fixed a custom slash command's embedded shell line running twice when a newer message interrupted the command while its prompt was being checked
  • Fixed --worktree sessions leaving a folder behind in .git/worktrees in repositories using git's reftable ref storage
  • Fixed claude self-hosted-runner sessions using Anthropic-managed git showing tracked files as staged deletions when starting in a reused clone whose remote is still empty
  • Fixed Ultracode not being announced to scheduled tasks and other delivered headless turns when ultracode is on in settings
  • Fixed MCP OAuth sign-in, token refresh and sign-out not sending configured headers/headersHelper values, which broke servers behind an authenticating proxy
  • Fixed the Artifact tool reporting a spurious one-line difference against the live page, and refusing the publish, when a large page with a line break after <head> is published again unchanged
  • Fixed $.ui.open reporting a mod's pane as placed in sessions where no surface draws it, such as Claude Code for VS Code and claude -p
  • Fixed the agent.spawn mod hook not running when a finished subagent or a killed teammate is resumed: the hook's event now carries resume, and a mod can refuse it
  • Fixed claude plugin validate rejecting a mod's $.state references when plugin.json has no types key and the contract is at ./types/index.d.ts
  • Fixed a mod's dimColor text looking the same as plain text under the dark ANSI theme and on 16-color terminals
  • Fixed plan mode running a write (an MCP tool's, a file's, a shell command's) that a PreToolUse hook or a mod's tool.check hook allowed
  • Fixed background subagents in auto mode sometimes sending their final report twice, once as the result and once as a message
  • Fixed SendMessage not finding a subagent by name after the CLI restarted and resumed the session (names given before the last compaction still need the agent ID)
  • Fixed replies cut off at the output token limit ending the turn silently, with no retry or error, after a request fell back to non-streaming mode
  • Fixed Read garbling UTF-16LE files with a byte-order mark, and Write dropping byte-order marks or silently converting Windows-1252, Shift-JIS, GBK or UTF-16BE files to UTF-8 (now refused)
  • Fixed cloud sessions sometimes leaving a message unanswered when the worker was replaced right after a compaction
  • Fixed cloud sessions and CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN sometimes answering a finished turn again after a restart, when a tool ended the turn and a skill loaded in the same step
  • Fixed photos sent over Remote Control being dropped when their copy could not be saved on your computer; Claude now still sees the photo
  • Fixed files sent over Remote Control sometimes not arriving in long-running sessions
  • Fixed files of 30 to 35 MiB sent over Remote Control or to a cloud session not arriving
  • Fixed a user-installed mod's $.env.set changing the environment or shell prefix that command hooks from managed settings start with
  • Windows: Fixed the process-liveness check leaving orphaned PowerShell processes behind on busy machines until memory ran out
  • Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks that set no shell failing open when Git for Windows isn't installed; a guard that fails now blocks the call
  • Windows: Fixed Bash commands failing with "command not found" for a whole session when Git Bash did not report its PATH at startup
  • Self-hosted runner: Improved what setup and doctor say when the runner's machine has no git credentials
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions that wrote output before their first turn being left with no release timer, ignoring --retire-at and delaying shutdown
  • Improved the error shown when a cloud session is refused because your claude.ai login was rejected or has expired: it now tells you to sign in again with claude auth login
  • Improved enforcement of managed permission rules, managed hooks and organization MCP tool names against user-installed mods
  • Improved memory and disk use when PDFs are @-mentioned: their bytes are no longer kept in the session transcript
  • Improved sandboxed Bash on Linux: Esc and Ctrl-C now work while wildcard read rules are being expanded for a command
  • Improved the startup warning for an unrecognized model ID: it is now one short line under the welcome banner with a docs link, instead of a long raw message
  • Improved the plugin-authoring skill's steps for sharing a mod: Claude asks public or private and checks the files before creating a GitHub repository
  • Improved the Skill tool's "Unknown skill" error to suggest a skill's listed name when Claude wrongly adds the anthropic-skills: prefix to it
  • Improved /reload-skills to say it re-sends the full skill list to Claude, which is how to get skills back after compaction
  • Improved the error shown when a worktree cannot be created because its base commit does not resolve: it now says how the lookup ended and the likely reasons, such as a repository without a commit
  • Improved the error for creating a worktree at a bare-repository layout's root: it now explains the layout instead of an unrelated git error
  • Improved artifact watching: a local session can now watch up to 25 published artifacts at once, up from 10
  • Improved background agent notifications: they now say when an agent is only waiting on its own background work, got a message too late for its result, or was stopped by a usage limit
  • Changed plugin hooks and workflow scripts to refuse values they hand back that nest deeper than 28,000 levels, with an error naming the limit (workflow scripts allowed 100,000)
  • Changed actions a plugin hook can block to be refused, not let through, when the hook cannot be handed them or cannot hand back its answer; a tool that already ran has its result withheld
  • Changed requests to claude.ai's connector proxy and to Anthropic-hosted MCP servers to no longer follow HTTP redirects; redirects by a connector's own server are unaffected
  • Changed MCP requests in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions to no longer follow HTTP redirects from the session's MCP proxy
  • Changed skill and command loading: one whose file or folder name has hidden, direction-changing or blank-like characters, < or > is no longer offered until renamed; such a name: is ignored
  • Changed ui.render trees in claude plugin test: each mod's Box or Text root now carries part: { plugin } naming the mod, so exact-tree assertions must include it
  • Changed WebFetch page reads to pick their effort as web searches do: the caller's level on the caller's own model, otherwise the level settings give the small model
  • Changed claude plugin test to fail a call to a mod's served $ method that has not answered within ten seconds, as a session does
  • Changed MCP allow rules to reach only the server they name: mcp__a no longer allows a server named a__b or a_; write mcp__<server>__* with the server's whole normalized name
  • Changed agent tools: lists to take only the named MCP server's tools; list a server whose name contains __ as mcp__<whole name>__*
  • Changed Claude in Chrome in Cowork cloud sessions outside auto mode: an approved-site action the safety classifier flags now asks you instead of being refused, unless managed settings apply
  • Changed cloud session and Remote Control MCP connectors to negotiate MCP protocol version 2026-07-28 by default on installs that fetch no flags; MCP_PROTOCOL_NEGOTIATION=legacy opts out
  • Changed MCP tool descriptions and server instructions from Anthropic's first-party MCP servers at api.anthropic.com to reach Claude in full instead of being cut at 4,096 characters
  • Changed auto mode in Cowork cloud sessions: a PermissionRequest hook can no longer approve shell commands or subagents; those prompts wait or are denied
  • Changed the resume command printed at exit: it names the session by its ID and no longer by its name, so that nothing in a session name can run when the line is pasted
  • Changed the resume command printed at exit of a worktree session: it uses -w and -r if the long flags do not fit the terminal. If neither fits a kept worktree, rows above it say where to run it
  • Changed /btw side questions in non-interactive sessions to return a timeout error when still unanswered after 11 minutes
  • Changed UserPromptSubmit hooks to run before a skill or custom slash command expands, so a hook that blocks the prompt now also stops its embedded shell commands
  • Changed a skill's own front-matter UserPromptSubmit hook to first run on the prompt after the one that invokes the skill
  • Changed the turn.start mod hook to also hear subagents' and teammates' turns, not only the main loop's; tell them apart by e.agentId (absent on the main loop)
  • Changed the errors shown when /ultrareview can't upload a repository to stop suggesting git add ., which could stage or commit untracked files such as .env
  • Changed the cyber safeguard notice to no longer ask people to apply to the Cyber Verification Program
  • [VSCode] Fixed an unsent prompt and its attachments being lost when switching to another session and back
  • [VSCode] Fixed unused blank chats keeping a background Claude process running after starting a new conversation
  • [VSCode] Fixed the mic button showing an internal error message when you are signed out of claude.ai; it now offers to sign you in
  • [VSCode] Improved startup time in workspaces without a Python environment by starting Claude while the Python extension loads
  • [VSCode] Improved startup: the model picker and slash command menu now fill in right away in a new window on a folder you've opened before
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a memory spike that could crash a session when many of its existing output files were re-sent to it at once
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed saving an edited routine silently moving it to a different environment when its own had been deleted or wasn't in the list; the routine now keeps its environment
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Sessions search in a self-hosted environment's admin details finding nothing when you paste the session ID from a session's link
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the Sessions and Runners lists in a self-hosted environment's admin details saying the list is empty when a search just has no matches
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the deploy command shown when you create a self-hosted environment or environment key: it shows in full, wraps between arguments, and has a visible copy button
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed deleting a self-hosted environment to turn off its routines right away, with the reason shown on each routine, instead of leaving their runs to fail
  • [Remote Control] Fixed Remote Control sessions whose computer can't be reached still appearing to send your messages; your text now stays in the box and Send is off until it reconnects
  • [Claude Tag] Added the ability for Claude in Slack to delete a canvas it created in a channel when someone asks it to
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack staying silent on untagged posts that a channel's own instructions tell it to answer, such as posts that tag someone else, in channels with guests
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack reporting a reply to another channel's thread as posted when it isn't a member there; it now says the reply wasn't delivered and how to fix that
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes ending a turn without posting its answer when a self-hosted runner's image has no python3
  • [Claude Tag] Changed how Claude in Slack corrects a message it got wrong: it edits the message in place and adds a short "Edited" note instead of striking through the old text
  • [Claude Tag] Changed Claude in Slack to join channels with more than 100 members quietly, with no intro message
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review's monthly spend-limit comment and check-run card sending admins to Claude Code settings; they now link the Usage page, where that limit is set

title: llm-gemini 0.35
summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.35

I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans. As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.)

Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:

The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.

Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.

One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.

When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.

(I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.)

Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars, here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles. That's a fun new twist!

title: Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems
summary:
Last week we announced that Gemini Enterprise has evolved to make it even simpler to get work done, and introduced the Gemini agent, your new universal agent for work. It's always on and ready to answer your questions. It will write code, complete longer and more complex tasks, or perform whatever you need to get the job done, all from a single prompt box. And model intelligence underpins it all.

To enable a new frontier of work, we are making our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, available on Google Cloud. 

We trained Argon to work with both depth and precision, which allows it to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks which are reinforced with strong domain expertise along the way. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like CodeMender, Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish. 

Four ways Argon changes how your business works

1. Hand off your hardest work

Your teams already use Gemini for business to answer questions and draft content. With Argon, they can hand off the deep, multi-step work that used to take hours or days, and get back finished work they can use.

Argon reads long documents that mix text, tables, charts and images, and turns them into one clear output grounded in those sources. It can pull findings from many sources into a single structured answer, analyze data over time, and write stronger legal, finance, and executive documents. On long tasks, it keeps going until the job is done. We trained Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause for confirmation before taking irreversible steps, and it tells you when it couldn't find something or finish a task.

Customers who tested Argon tell us it excels at turning huge, unstructured inputs into cohesive outputs. 

"As software development becomes more agentic, teams need models that can support long-running, multi-step work across all stages of the development lifecycle. Gemini 4 Argon is designed to help organizations bring AI into development, security, and operations while keeping it within established enterprise workflows and controls.” – Stuart Moncada, VP, GitLab.

2. Precise, verifiable results on the work that drives your business

In finance, legal, tax, and other regulated work, calculations and data extraction need to be precise, repeatable, and verifiable. 

For financial quantitative work, Argon can help automate multi-step ledger reconciliations, spreadsheet formulas, and variance analyses. It delivers high calculation integrity, citation fidelity, and formula accuracy across quantitative models. The proof is in the numbers: Argon leads on the Vals Index, which measures economic impact across finance, coding, legal, and tax work.

In legal research, Argon can help legal teams review case law and regulatory filings to pull out verified citations and key precedents. It leads on domain-specific evaluations like Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark for legal research and drafting, with strong citation fidelity and direct answers when helping teams evaluate complex legal precedents. 

"Gemini 4 Argon shows how much progress Google has made on agentic legal reasoning. We saw substantial improvements over Gemini 3.1 Pro across our legal agent evaluations, particularly in corporate M&A, data privacy and cybersecurity, and EC/VC. Accuracy also held up on long-document analysis, an encouraging result for lawyers working through detailed transactional matters." – Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research, Harvey.

“We collaborated with Google on NowAI-Bench to help shape Gemini 4 for key enterprise work. In early access, it delivered roughly 20% improved task success than Gemini 3.8 Flash, with standout gains in HR and customer service. On the ServiceNow AI Platform, our L1 Service Desk AI specialist brings Google’s most advanced intelligence, governed and secure, turning tasks into fully autonomous work.” - Nenshad Bardoliwalla, Senior Vice President, AI Products, ServiceNow.

3. Build and ship products faster

Argon is built to handle complex, multi-step projects from start to finish. Our customers consistently ask for intelligence that can break down goals, track progress, and update multiple files at the same time.

"Gemini 4 Argon handles complex tasks reliably, from 3D games to rich animations. In Figma Make, it helps teams turn their most ambitious, multi-step ideas into impressive prototypes.” – Loredana Crisan, Chief Design Officer, Figma. 

To see how well Argon handles this, we put it to work on our own tools. The team behind our open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK) set out to reduce framework overhead and improve code performance while maintaining full compatibility with existing applications. Working autonomously overnight within automated testing guardrails, Argon surfaced optimizations, now live in google/adk-python, that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and speed up cold imports by 21%. To learn more, read the engineering deep dive here.

Across Google, engineering teams using Argon in Google Antigravity have increased agentic code submissions by more than 35% while cutting code rollbacks by nearly a third. The Chrome team used Argon to finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files in Chromium's 40 million-line codebase, completing months of work in weeks. Argon's improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision and visual coding also make it faster to go from idea to working prototype. 

For more advanced algorithms, our code optimization and discovery agent AlphaEvolve uses Argon to deliver strong performance improvements across real-world enterprise workloads, including factory scheduling, logistics, game code speed-ups, and chip layout — as well as complex mathematical benchmarks, and more. 

To learn how to best use Argon, check out the developer's guide.

4. Stronger defense for your code and business 

While Argon has cyber mitigations that block offensive tasks such as pentesting and exploitation, you can still take full advantage of Argon’s defensive capabilities using CodeMender to find and fix vulnerabilities, or use Argon with your own security harness. It ties for first place on CWE-Bench v1 with a top score of 68% for remediating security vulnerabilities.

"We are integrating Gemini 4 Argon into MarketingX for automated codebase security audits. In our evaluations, the model successfully identified 100% of top-priority vulnerabilities with 0% fabricated vulnerabilities across verified claims. This precision unlocks proactive, code-level security for our customers before deployment.” - Yunus Emre, Chief AI Officer of AI Lab, HubX.

Security also means being able to trust Argon inside your own environment. Argon is our most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections, where malicious instructions or context are used to hijack a model’s behavior. It leads the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, cutting attack success across 15 adaptive attempts to 0.7%. That matters when Argon reads email, documents and webpages that may contain hidden malicious instructions. 

We are also releasing Argon without cyber guardrails to a select set of trusted defenders, which allows for testing a full breadth of cybersecurity capabilities. Trusted defenders are vetted through our Fairwind Program, a limited access initiative that provides government, critical infrastructure, and cybersecurity partners exclusive, unmitigated access to advanced  models. 

Enterprise customers and partners in our early access program are already seeing strong wins with Argon.

Leaders from Amplitude, Deloitte, and Rakuten share Gemini 4 Argon results

Get started

Starting today, Gemini 4 Argon is available in Gemini for business on the web, desktop, and mobile. Enterprise developers and builders can access Argon via API in Gemini platform under model ID gemini-4-argon, in Google AI Studio, and in Google Antigravity.

Argon launches at an introductory rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off. After November 30, standard pricing of $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens will apply. Review the model card and developer guide for complete technical specifications, token limits, and migration instructions.

Cyber defenders can join us at Security Summit to learn how to use Gemini 4 Argon to defend against machine-speed threats and automate remediation.

title: Quoting Geoffrey Huntley
summary:
If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten.

— Geoffrey Huntley, nobody should type code by hand anymore. here's what's left.
